abraham-h-cannon-1859.life_summary: Abraham Hoagland Cannon was born on March 12, 1859, in Salt Lake City, Utah Territory, to George Q. Cannon, a prominent Latter-day Saint apostle, and Elizabeth Hoagland. Growing up in an elite Church family gave him advantages and expectations. He demonstrated early aptitude in architectural studies under Obed Taylor at Deseret University, combining aesthetic sensibility with technical knowledge. Cannon also showed entrepreneurial acumen and literary interest, advancing rapidly in positions of responsibility. His education and family connections positioned him for significant influence in Church affairs. However, his life was marked by legal challenges stemming from his practice of plural marriage at a time when the Church was under intense federal scrutiny.
abraham-h-cannon-1859.church_summary: Abraham H. Cannon became a member of the First Seven Presidents of the Seventy on October 9, 1882, at age 23. He assumed control of the Juvenile Instructor that same year, serving as editor and publisher. In October 1892, he took control of the Deseret News with his brother John Q. Cannon, and also served as editor and publisher of The Contributor. He was ordained to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles on October 7, 1889, by Joseph F. Smith. On March 17, 1886, he was convicted under the Edmunds Act for unlawful cohabitation, receiving a six-month sentence and $300 fine, but was pardoned by President Grover Cleveland in 1894. He died on July 19, 1896, at age 37, from an ear infection that developed after exposure to ocean water during a California visit.
abraham-h-cannon-1859.birth_place: Salt Lake City, Utah Territory, United States
abraham-h-cannon-1859.death_place: Salt Lake City, Utah, United States
abraham-h-cannon-1859.burial_place: Salt Lake City Cemetery, Salt Lake City, Utah

abraham-o-woodruff-1872.life_summary: Abraham Owen Woodruff was born on November 23, 1872, near Salt Lake City, Utah Territory, into the prominent Woodruff family, son of the Church president. Growing up with direct access to the highest levels of Church leadership shaped his worldview and instilled in him a sense of responsibility. As a young man, he demonstrated exceptional entrepreneurial abilities and vision for community development. In 1900, he spearheaded the establishment of a significant Mormon colony at Bighorn Basin, Wyoming, orchestrating the purchase of 18,000 acres under the Carey Act and serving as president of the Big Horn Basin Colonization Company. Through his efforts, over 500 Latter-day Saints were settled in the region, demonstrating his organizational prowess and commitment to Church expansion.
abraham-o-woodruff-1872.church_summary: Abraham O. Woodruff served a mission in the Swiss-German Mission from 1893 to 1896, during which he faced persecution and conducted secret preaching in Frankfurt, Dresden (where he served as branch president), and Berlin. At age 24, he was ordained an apostle on October 7, 1897, becoming the youngest member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles at that time. He married Helen May Winters on June 30, 1896, and later entered into a plural marriage with Eliza Avery Clark in 1901, keeping the second marriage secret. His apostolic career was tragically cut short when he died on June 20, 1904, at age 31, from smallpox contracted in El Paso, Texas. Helen died just thirteen days earlier on June 7, fulfilling a prophecy that they would not be separated in death by more than two weeks.
abraham-o-woodruff-1872.birth_place: near Salt Lake City, Utah Territory, United States
abraham-o-woodruff-1872.burial_place: Salt Lake City Cemetery, Salt Lake City, Utah

adam-s-bennion-1886.life_summary: Adam Samuel Bennion was born on December 2, 1886, in Taylorsville, Utah Territory. He grew up in the Salt Lake Valley during a period of significant Church development and community building. Bennion pursued advanced education and became deeply involved in religious instruction and education. He married Minerva Richards Young, and together they had three sons and two daughters. Before his prominent Church appointment, Bennion established himself as an educational leader and author of religious instruction materials. His publications, including Principles of Teaching (1921) and What It Means to Be a Mormon (1917), reflected his commitment to developing both pedagogical methods and doctrinal clarity. His life embodied the integration of intellectual rigor with spiritual conviction.
adam-s-bennion-1886.church_summary: Bennion served as superintendent of LDS Church Schools and played a central role in expanding the seminary program, which provided religious instruction to youth throughout the Church. He authored extensively on religious principles and trained seminary teachers in effective pedagogical methods. On April 9, 1953, he was called to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles by President David O. McKay. Despite his call coming late in his life, Bennion served with energy and dedication until his death on February 11, 1958, roughly five years after his ordination as an apostle. His tenure was brief but meaningful, bringing decades of educational expertise to the apostolic office.

albert-carrington-1813.life_summary: Albert Carrington was born January 8, 1813, in Royalton, Vermont, and received an excellent education for his era, graduating from Dartmouth College in 1833. Before joining the LDS Church, he worked as a schoolteacher and studied law in Pennsylvania, demonstrating both intellectual ambition and professional capability. Carrington was baptized into the Latter-day Saint movement on July 18, 1841, in Wiota, Wisconsin, at age twenty-eight, after the main body of the church had already established itself in Missouri and Illinois. He married Rhoda Maria Woods in 1839 and later took Mary Rock as a plural wife in January 1846. Carrington brought his education and professional training into church service, becoming one of the church's earliest intellectual and administrative leaders.
albert-carrington-1813.church_summary: Carrington served as editor of the Deseret News during two separate periods (1854–1856 and 1862–1867) and was a member of the Utah Territorial Legislative Council. He was appointed the tenth Church Historian in 1871 and served until 1874, working to document and preserve early church records. He became a member of the Quorum of the Twelve in 1870 and served multiple times as President of the European Mission (1871–1873, 1875–1877, 1880–1882). He was also called as a Counselor in the First Presidency from 1873 to 1877. However, Carrington's later years were marked by controversy; he was excommunicated on November 6, 1885, for what the church termed adultery and lewd conduct. He was rebaptized on November 1, 1887, but was not reinstated to apostolic office.

albert-e-bowen-1875.life_summary: Albert Edward Bowen was born on October 31, 1875, in Henderson Creek, Idaho Territory, during the frontier period of LDS settlement. He grew up in the rapidly developing Utah communities and received his education in the Salt Lake Valley. Before his church prominence, Bowen worked in business and established himself as a community leader. He was married twice: first to Aletha Reeder in 1902, who died in 1906, and then to Emma Lucy Gates in 1916, with whom he remained until her death in 1951. His life spanned from the territorial era through the mid-twentieth century, witnessing dramatic transformations in the Church and American society.
albert-e-bowen-1875.church_summary: Bowen served as a missionary in Switzerland and Germany from 1902 to 1904. He was ordained to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 1921 and served in that capacity until his death in 1953. Throughout his ecclesiastical career, Bowen was deeply committed to the welfare of the poor and infirm, advocating that the Church maintain robust charitable traditions even as members became more prosperous. He also became known for defending the historical reputation of Joseph Smith against what he called poisonous slander in secular biographical scholarship. His thirty-two years as an apostle shaped Church welfare policies and historical scholarship.
teaching_emphasis: Care for the poor and infirm
Economic prosperity balanced with charitable duty
Defense of Joseph Smith's historical legacy
Opposition to secular slander against the Founder

alonzo-a-hinckley-1870.life_summary: Alonzo Arza Hinckley was born April 23, 1870, in Cove Fort, Utah Territory, in the heart of Mormon country. He grew up in a frontier community and developed practical skills in agriculture, husbandry, and community management. Before his ecclesiastical prominence, Hinckley established himself as a reliable leader in his local community, managing property and participating in the cooperative institutions that characterized Mormon economic life. He demonstrated the steady temperament and administrative competence required for leadership in the Church's stake system. His rise to prominence reflected the Church's practice of promoting from within, identifying capable leaders from among the faithful laity who had proven themselves through decades of faithful service.
alonzo-a-hinckley-1870.church_summary: Hinckley served a mission to the Netherlands and subsequently became president of the Deseret Stake in 1912, overseeing a region in western Millard County, Utah. On October 11, 1934, he was ordained an apostle to fill a vacancy created by David O. McKay's elevation to the First Presidency. Though his tenure in the Quorum of the Twelve was brief—he died December 22, 1936, from stomach cancer—he represented the Church's commitment to maintaining succession and developed the leadership of younger apostles. His service demonstrated that the Church valued steady, proven administrators who had earned trust through long years of faithful community leadership.

alvin-r-dyer-1903.life_summary: Alvin Ray Dyer was born on January 1, 1903, in Salt Lake City, Utah, during the early decades of twentieth-century Mormonism. He married May Elizabeth Jackson in the Salt Lake Temple in 1926, establishing a partnership that would sustain him throughout his church service career. Dyer grew up in the post-pioneering era of the church, coming of age during the consolidation of the LDS institution in the American West. He devoted much of his life to church administrative work and missionary oversight, building a career focused on expansion and institutional efficiency rather than theological innovation or literary contribution.
alvin-r-dyer-1903.church_summary: Dyer served as a missionary in the Eastern States Mission from 1922 to 1924, and later rose to more prominent leadership positions. He became Central States Mission president beginning in 1954, and subsequently served as European Mission president from 1960 to 1962. Dyer became known for his emphasis on missionary efficiency, promoting rapid conversion instruction and famously stating that all essential truths could be taught in less than three minutes. In 1961, he articulated controversial racial doctrine regarding Black church members, attributing priesthood restrictions to descent from Cain. Dyer also supported the Baseball Baptism Program to accelerate youth baptisms. He died on March 6, 1977, in Salt Lake City, having spent over half a century in missionary and ecclesiastical administration.

mission.location: Eastern States, Central States, and Europe

amasa-m-lyman-1813.life_summary: Amasa Mason Lyman was born in 1813 and became a prominent leader during the Church's formative years. He was introduced to the faith by missionaries in spring 1832 and baptized on April 27, 1832. Lyman participated fully in the Church's westward expansion, helping to establish the San Bernardino settlement in California, where he served as the settlement's first mayor. He purchased land as part of the Rancho San Bernardino acquisition and contributed to Mormon colonization efforts in the West. His family became influential within Church leadership circles, with descendants who achieved prominence in subsequent generations.
amasa-m-lyman-1813.church_summary: Lyman joined the First Quorum of the Seventy in 1835 and served as regent of the University of Nauvoo in 1841. Joseph Smith called him to the apostolate in 1842 and appointed him as an additional counselor in the First Presidency in 1843. Following Smith's death, Lyman supported Brigham Young's leadership and participated in the 1847 westward migration. However, his Church status declined after he preached doctrinal positions at odds with established teaching. The Church stripped him of apostleship in 1867 and excommunicated him in 1870 for associating with dissident groups, though he was posthumously reinstated in 1909.

anthon-h-lund-1844.life_summary: Anthon Henrik Lund was born on May 15, 1844, in Aalborg, Denmark. He immigrated to the United States in 1862 with his grandmother, settling in Sanpete County, Utah Territory. Growing up in Scandinavia and then pioneering in Utah, Lund developed a multilingual fluency and cultural sophistication that distinguished him among Church leaders. He married Sarah Ann Peterson in 1870 and raised a family while advancing rapidly in ecclesiastical responsibility. Lund became known as the first apostle since the early days of the Church to eschew plural marriage, a significant distinction during his era. His intellectual abilities and linguistic skills made him invaluable to Church administration during a formative period.
anthon-h-lund-1844.church_summary: Anthon H. Lund was ordained to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles on October 7, 1889, becoming the first apostle whose native language was not English. He served as president of Manti Temple beginning in 1891 and later as president of Salt Lake Temple from 1911 to 1921. He was appointed Second Counselor in the First Presidency on October 17, 1901, serving until April 7, 1910, when he was promoted to First Counselor, a position he held until his death on March 2, 1921. He also served as President of the Quorum of the Twelve from 1918 to 1921. Additionally, he served as Church Historian from 1900 to 1921, directing crucial historical and archival work. He organized the Turkish Mission in 1897 and served as president of the Scandinavian Mission (1884-1885) and European Mission (1893-1896).
anthon-h-lund-1844.death_place: Salt Lake City, Utah, United States
anthon-h-lund-1844.burial_place: Salt Lake City Cemetery, Salt Lake City, Utah

anthony-w-ivins-1852.life_summary: Anthony Woodward Ivins was born September 16, 1852, in Toms River, New Jersey, to parents who had recently joined the LDS Church. His youth was marked by westward migration and pioneering life in the American frontier, settling in southern Utah. He developed practical skills in agriculture, land management, and indigenous relations that distinguished his career. Before his ecclesiastical prominence, Ivins served as mayor of St. George and as a prosecuting attorney and assessor, building a reputation as an able administrator and defender of Church interests. His intimate knowledge of southwestern frontier conditions and his diplomatic abilities made him a natural choice for leadership in developing the Church's Mexican communities and indigenous missionary work.
anthony-w-ivins-1852.church_summary: Ivins served multiple missions to the American Southwest and Mexico (1875, 1877, 1882–1884), eventually becoming the first stake president in Mexico and overseer of Mexican Church affairs. He was ordained an apostle on October 6, 1907, and served in the Quorum of the Twelve until 1921, then as Second Counselor to Heber J. Grant (1921) and First Counselor (1925–1934). His mission work and presidency of the Southern States Mission established him as a bridge between the Anglo Mormon hierarchy and Spanish-speaking and Native American populations. He dedicated vast territories for missionary work and pioneered Church expansion into Mexico and the American South.
teaching_emphasis: Indigenous relations and Native American missionary efforts

boyd-k-packer-1924.life_summary: Boyd Kimball Packer was born September 10, 1924, in Brigham City, Utah, to a farming family with deep LDS Church roots. He served as a missionary in the New England States before studying at Brigham Young University. After college, Packer worked as an educator, becoming a high school principal and later a faculty member at BYU. His professional background in education and administration shaped his approach to church leadership. He married Donna Smith in 1947, and together they raised ten children, including his son Allan F. Packer, who also became a general authority. Packer remained active in educational reform and church growth initiatives throughout his adult life.
boyd-k-packer-1924.church_summary: Packer served as a general authority from 1961 until his death in 2015, advancing to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 1970. He became Acting President of the Quorum in 1994 and President in 2008, serving in that capacity longer than any previous holder. He dedicated the Ukraine for gospel preaching in 1991 and oversaw the dedications of the San Diego California, Regina Saskatchewan, and Brigham City Utah temples. Packer's ministry emphasized the spiritual power of hymn-centered worship, the principle of 'rule before exception,' and the importance of personal spiritual promptings in moral development and church leadership.

brigham-young-1801.life_summary: Brigham Young was born on June 1, 1801, in Whitingham, Vermont, to a farming family in rural New England. He received limited formal education but developed practical skills in carpentry and various trades. Young worked as a carpenter and craftsman before his conversion to the LDS faith. He lived and worked in upstate New York before joining the growing Mormon community. Young eventually became a master organizer and builder, overseeing major construction projects and settlement efforts. His leadership abilities extended beyond religious matters into civic administration, economic development, and territorial governance. Young led the westward migration of the Mormon community along the Mormon Trail from 1846 to 1847, establishing Salt Lake Valley as the new center for the LDS faith.
brigham-young-1801.church_summary: Brigham Young served multiple missionary tours to the eastern United States beginning in 1835, and undertook a significant one-year mission to the United Kingdom where he organized church publishing efforts. He was a key lieutenant to Joseph Smith and played instrumental roles in the development of the Kirtland and Nauvoo temples. After Joseph Smith's death, Young emerged as the primary leader of the LDS Church and directed the westward migration to Utah in 1846–1847. He designated the location of the Salt Lake Temple just four days after arriving in Salt Lake Valley and oversaw construction of the Salt Lake Tabernacle and announced plans for the St. George, Manti, and Logan temples. Young served as President of the LDS Church from 1847 until his death in 1877.
brigham-young-1801.burial_place: Mormon Pioneer Memorial Monument grounds, Salt Lake City

brigham-young-jr-1836.life_summary: Brigham Young Jr. was born on December 18, 1836, in Kirtland, Ohio, as the eldest son of Brigham Young. He grew up during the formative years of the LDS Church, experiencing the communities of Kirtland, Nauvoo, and finally Salt Lake City. Young Jr. received his education through church schools and practical training in leadership and administration under his father's guidance. He married Catherine Curtis Spencer on November 15, 1855, and subsequently married Jane Carrington in 1857 and Abigail Stevens in an undated ceremony. Young Jr. established himself as a church leader in his own right, taking responsibility for important institutional development projects. He was instrumental in founding the Deseret Sunday School Union in 1867 and overseeing western colonization efforts across Utah, Wyoming, and Arizona.
brigham-young-jr-1836.church_summary: Brigham Young Jr. served as a missionary in England from 1862 to 1863, where he worked in London and accompanied Joseph F. Smith to Paris. He returned to Europe as assistant to mission president Daniel H. Wells from 1864 to 1867, then succeeded Wells as European Mission president in 1865. Young Jr. served a second tenure as European Mission president from 1890 to 1893, headquartered in Liverpool. In 1877, he joined Erastus Snow and Wilford Woodruff in dedicating portions of the St. George Temple. His ecclesiastical roles centered on centralized missionary coordination, regional church administration, and institutional development. Young Jr. edited the Deseret News from 1877 to 1880 and established settlements in Cache Valley, Star Valley (Wyoming), and Arizona.
teaching_emphasis: Colonization and settlement of western territories
Sunday School education and youth development

bruce-r-mcconkie-1915.life_summary: Bruce Redd McConkie was born on July 29, 1915, in Ann Arbor, Michigan, into a family that would shape his theological legacy. He married Amelia Smith on October 13, 1937, at the Salt Lake Temple; Amelia was the daughter of Joseph Fielding Smith, who would later serve as president of the LDS Church. This significant family connection positioned McConkie within the church's highest ecclesiastical circles from the outset of his marriage. McConkie developed into one of the most prolific and influential theological voices in twentieth-century Mormonism, known for his systematic approach to scriptural interpretation and doctrinal formulation.
bruce-r-mcconkie-1915.church_summary: McConkie served in two significant missionary capacities: the Eastern States Mission from September 1934 to 1937, serving in Pennsylvania and New York including at Hill Cumorah, and the Southern Australian Mission from February 1961 to 1964 as mission president. He rose to apostolic prominence and became known for his authoritative doctrinal teaching, famously stating 'it is my province to teach to the church what the doctrine is.' McConkie emphasized scriptural interpretation, the nature of Christ and messianic theology, and encouraged leaders to listen for the whisperings of the Holy Ghost. He died on April 19, 1985, at age 69, ending a tenure marked by doctrinal precision and spiritual authority.

mission.location: Eastern States Mission and Southern Australia

teaching_emphasis: spiritual humility and Holy Ghost guidance

charles-a-callis-1865.life_summary: Charles Albert Callis was born May 4, 1865, in Dublin, Ireland, to a family that converted to Mormonism during the great Irish missionary movement of the nineteenth century. At age 16, he entered coal mining, enduring eleven years of hazardous labor in Utah mines before pivoting toward legal and civic pursuits. His experiences as a laborer and a man of the frontier gave him deep empathy for working-class communities and an understanding of their struggles. He eventually earned admission to the Florida bar and developed an extensive legal practice defending Church interests, particularly protecting LDS missionaries in hostile environments of the American South. His trajectory from miner to attorney reflected personal determination and the Church's capacity to develop leadership from humble origins.
charles-a-callis-1865.church_summary: Callis served missions to Wyoming, the British Isles (1892–1895), Iowa, and Florida, eventually becoming Southern States Mission President (1908–1933), overseeing 250 missionaries across ten states. He was ordained an apostle on October 12, 1933, joining the Quorum of the Twelve in his final years. Through legal advocacy and missionary administration, he expanded Church presence in difficult territory and protected the religious freedom of Latter-day Saints in the segregated South. His published work, Fundamentals of Religion, compiled radio lectures on LDS doctrine. He excelled at both administrative detail and public oratory, earning respect for his integrity and his unwavering commitment to conscience and righteousness.

mission.location: Southern United States and British Isles

charles-w-penrose-1832.life_summary: Charles W. Penrose was born February 4, 1832, in Camberwell, London, England, into a Protestant family that embraced the LDS faith in the 1840s. Raised in an environment of religious conviction and intellectual discourse, Penrose developed skills in composition, rhetoric, and theological reflection that would define his public ministry. Before his full-time church service, he worked as a printer and journalist in England, establishing himself as an able writer and editor. He emigrated to Utah in the 1860s, where he continued his dual pursuits of journalism and religious leadership, becoming deeply involved in Church educational and publishing endeavors.
charles-w-penrose-1832.church_summary: Penrose served a seven-year English mission in his youth and later presided over the Church's Lancashire operations (1865–1868) and European missions (1906–1910). Ordained to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 1904, he served until 1911, then became Second Counselor to Joseph F. Smith (1911–1918) and First Counselor to Heber J. Grant (1918–1925). As editor-in-chief of the Deseret News and theology professor at Brigham Young Academy, he shaped Mormon discourse on doctrine and literary expression. He also authored numerous LDS hymns, including 'Up, Awake, Ye Defenders of Zion,' embedding theological themes into the Church's musical tradition.
teaching_emphasis: Journalism and public relations for the Church

clark-g-gilbert-1970.life_summary: Clark G. Gilbert was born on June 18, 1970, in Oakland, California, and grew up in the San Francisco Bay Area. He received his education and developed expertise in organizational leadership and academic administration. After completing his undergraduate studies, Gilbert served as a full-time missionary for the Latter-day Saint Church in Kobe, Japan, from 1989 to 1991, where he gained cross-cultural experience and deepened his commitment to church principles. Upon returning home, he married Christine Gilbert in 1994 at the Salt Lake Temple, and they established a family with eight children. His professional expertise in higher education and organizational development positioned him for leadership roles within church institutions.
clark-g-gilbert-1970.church_summary: Gilbert served as Church Commissioner of Education, where he championed the cause of maintaining religious distinction in Latter-day Saint universities. His tenure focused on preserving what he termed 'the distinctive light of religious universities' and resisting pressures from the wider American academy to conform to secular ideals. Drawing on the work of scholars like James Tunstead Burtchaell, Gilbert emphasized alignment between academic institutions and church doctrinal teachings on marriage, family, and gender—ensuring that religious colleges remained authentic expressions of faith-centered education.

d-todd-christofferson-1945.life_summary: Delbert Todd Christofferson was born on January 24, 1945, in American Fork, Utah. He grew up in the Intermountain West and pursued legal studies, eventually earning a law degree. Christofferson's professional career included a notable position as law clerk to U.S. Federal Judge John Sirica during the Watergate scandal (1972–1974), where he witnessed firsthand the constitutional and legal complexities surrounding one of America's greatest political crises. He worked as an attorney in Salt Lake City before dedicating himself to full-time Church service. In 1968, he married Katherine Jacob at the Salt Lake Temple, and the couple raised five children together while building a life centered on both professional accomplishment and deep religious commitment.
d-todd-christofferson-1945.church_summary: Christofferson served in a two-year mission to Argentina under mission president Richard G. Scott before pursuing legal studies. He was called as a member of the Presidency of the Seventy and later as a member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 2009. His ministry has included significant work on family history and sensitive negotiations with Jewish leaders regarding Church policies on temple work for Holocaust victims, demonstrating his commitment to both theological integrity and interfaith respect. His legal background has informed his approach to policy matters within the Church administration, and his teachings have emphasized the importance of family relationships and eternal covenants.

dale-g-renlund-1952.life_summary: Dale Grant Renlund was born on November 13, 1952, in Salt Lake City, Utah. He pursued advanced education in medicine, eventually earning his medical degree and establishing himself as a respected cardiologist and physician. Before his appointment to full-time Church leadership, Renlund enjoyed a distinguished medical career, combining his professional expertise with active ecclesiastical involvement. His medical background provided him with scientific knowledge and practical experience in health and human wellbeing. In 1977, he married Ruth Lybbert, and together they established a family while balancing his demanding medical practice with significant Church responsibilities and volunteer service.
dale-g-renlund-1952.church_summary: Renlund served as a full-time missionary in Sweden from 1972 to 1974, where he developed proficiency in Scandinavian languages and culture. He was called to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 2015. In April 2019, he dedicated the Kinshasa Democratic Republic of the Congo Temple. His ministry has emphasized religious freedom and its societal benefits, mental health and suicide prevention, religion's role in improving individual health, and youth engagement through digital platforms. His unique combination of medical knowledge and spiritual authority has allowed him to address contemporary challenges facing members, particularly regarding mental health awareness and personal wellbeing.
dale-g-renlund-1952.birth_place: Salt Lake City, Utah, United States
temples_dedicated: Kinshasa Democratic Republic of the Congo Temple (2019)
teaching_emphasis: Religious freedom and its societal benefits
Religion's role in improving individual health

dallin-h-oaks-1932.life_summary: Dallin Harris Oaks was born on August 12, 1932, in Provo, Utah. He earned his bachelor's degree in accounting from Brigham Young University in 1954 and pursued advanced legal education at the University of Chicago Law School on scholarship, graduating with a J.D. in 1957. As a law student, he served as editor-in-chief of the University of Chicago Law Review. Following law school, Oaks clerked for Chief Justice Earl Warren from 1957 to 1958, an experience that shaped his constitutional law thinking. He practiced corporate litigation at Kirkland & Ellis before joining the University of Chicago's law faculty, where he specialized in constitutional law and evidence.
dallin-h-oaks-1932.church_summary: Oaks served as BYU's eighth president from 1971 to 1980, overseeing the creation of the law school and business school while promoting affirmative action policies and emphasizing the equal treatment of women in the workplace. He served on the Utah Supreme Court from 1980 to 1984 before joining the Church's Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 1984. Presidents Gerald Ford and Ronald Reagan both considered him for appointment to the U.S. Supreme Court—Ford in 1975 and Reagan in 1981—though neither appointment was ultimately made. Oaks became president of the Church in October 2025 following Russell M. Nelson's death.

daniel-h-wells-1814.life_summary: Daniel Hanmer Wells was born on October 27, 1814, in Trenton, New York. He entered matrimony multiple times over his lifetime, marrying seven women between 1837 and 1871, including Eliza Rebecca Robison, Louisa Free, Martha Givens Harris, Lydia Ann Alley, Susan Hannah Alley, Hannah Corilla Free, Emmeline Blanche Woodward, and Hannah Tupper. This pattern of marriage was not unusual among prominent nineteenth-century church leaders engaged in plural marriage. Wells established himself as a major figure in the development of Salt Lake City and the Latter-day Saint community, serving in both ecclesiastical and civic capacities that shaped the nascent Utah Territory.
daniel-h-wells-1814.church_summary: Wells served as president of the European Mission of the LDS Church on two separate occasions: from 1864 to 1865 and again from 1884 to 1887, establishing himself as a trusted leader in international church administration. He dedicated the St. George Temple on April 6, 1877, and served as the first president of the Manti Utah Temple from 1888 to 1891. Beyond his religious roles, Wells superintended public works for the church from 1848 to 1863, overseeing construction of the Salt Lake Temple and Salt Lake Tabernacle—monumental projects that defined Salt Lake City's development. He served as the third mayor of Salt Lake City, exercising significant civic authority. Wells died on March 24, 1891, having spent more than four decades in positions of ecclesiastical and civil leadership.

david-a-bednar-1952.life_summary: David Allan Bednar was born on June 15, 1952, in Oakland, California. He grew up in California and received his undergraduate education before pursuing higher learning that prepared him for scholarly and ecclesiastical roles. Before his appointment to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, Bednar served as a university administrator and religious educator, earning recognition for his work in Church education. His academic background combined with his deep religious commitment positioned him as a thoughtful voice in the Church. In 1975, he married Susan Kae Robinson at the Salt Lake Temple, and the couple built their family while he advanced through various leadership and educational positions within the Church structure.
david-a-bednar-1952.church_summary: Bednar served as president of Brigham Young University-Idaho before his 2004 appointment to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles. He has emphasized spiritual development, revelation, meekness, perseverance, joy, and prayer as central to faithful discipleship. His teaching focuses on accessing living water through personal revelation and understanding things as they really are. He dedicated the Star Valley Wyoming Temple in 2016 and participated in the 2019 dedication of the Rome Italy Temple alongside his fellow apostles. His ministry has centered on helping members develop deeper spiritual understanding and a more intimate relationship with divine revelation.

david-b-haight-1906.life_summary: David Bruce Haight was born on September 2, 1906, in Oakley, Idaho, a rural community in the northern part of the state. He married Ruby M. Olson, and the couple spent much of their married life in California, where Haight established himself as a respected civic leader and businessman. He served as mayor of Palo Alto, California, a position of considerable prominence in the San Francisco Bay Area's development during the mid-twentieth century. Haight's commitment to his community was so strong that he initially resisted accepting higher church responsibilities that would require him to relinquish his mayoral post.
david-b-haight-1906.church_summary: Haight served as president of the LDS Church's mission in Scotland, an appointment that required him to resign from his position as mayor of Palo Alto despite objections from the city council. He was ordained an apostle on January 8, 1976, becoming a member of the church's Quorum of the Twelve Apostles. Haight achieved the distinction of becoming the oldest apostle in church history until being surpassed by Russell M. Nelson in 2022. He died on July 31, 2004, at an advanced age, having served faithfully in his apostolic role for nearly three decades.

david-o-mckay-1873.life_summary: David Oman McKay was born September 8, 1873, on a farm in Huntsville, Utah Territory, to Scottish and Welsh immigrant parents who brought Old World culture and values to frontier Utah. His father, a Scottish emigrant from Caithness, and his mother, a Welsh immigrant from Merthyr Tydfil, created a household valuing education, music, and intellectual refinement. McKay attended Brigham Young Academy and later the University of Utah, becoming well-educated for his generation. He served as a teacher and educator before his ecclesiastical service, and traveled extensively throughout his life, developing a cosmopolitan perspective. McKay's personal charisma, distinguished appearance with his white hair, and thoughtful demeanor made him a recognizable public figure.
david-o-mckay-1873.church_summary: McKay served missions to Great Britain (1897–1899), presiding over the Scottish district, and conducted a worldwide tour (1920–1921) covering Hawaii, Samoa, Tonga, New Zealand, and Palestine. He served as European Mission president (1923–1925) from London. Ordained an apostle in 1906, he became counselor to church presidents and president in 1951, leading until his death in 1970. McKay popularized 'every member a missionary,' emphasizing home-centered faith. His famous teaching 'no other success can compensate for failure in the home' shaped generations of Mormon family values. He stressed education, combated communism, and implemented priesthood correlation programs.

david-w-patten-1799.life_summary: David Wight Patten was born on November 14, 1799, in Vermont, growing up during the early federal period in New England. Little is recorded of his family background or early life, but he demonstrated a spiritual inclination that drew him toward religious exploration. In 1828, he married Phoebe Ann Babcock, and together they established their household. Patten lived through significant periods of American westward expansion and religious awakening, the very currents that would define his spiritual journey and ministerial calling.
david-w-patten-1799.church_summary: Patten was baptized early in the church's history and quickly became one of its most active missionaries. He served twelve short missions during 1832–1833 and again in Tennessee in 1834, and was numbered among the first missionaries to visit the southern United States. His evangelical efforts were remarkably successful: he converted approximately eighty people in Henderson, New York, and baptized roughly 130 total throughout his service. Patten was ordained an apostle on February 15, 1835, by Oliver Cowdery, David Whitmer, and Martin Harris. He was known for emphasizing faith healing and miracles, laying hands on the sick in Christ-like ministry. He served as an apostle until his death on October 25, 1838, in Ray County, Missouri, making him one of the earliest casualties in the church's troubled Missouri period.

delbert-l-stapley-1896.life_summary: Delbert Llewellyn Stapley was born on December 11, 1896, in Mesa, Arizona Territory, during the early days of Arizona settlement. He grew up in the Arizona LDS community and received his education in territorial schools. Stapley developed a strong commitment to community service and religious duty from an early age. During World War I, he served with distinction in the U.S. Marine Corps, demonstrating patriotic commitment alongside his religious convictions. Despite being offered a contract with Major League Baseball, Stapley declined to pursue missionary service, prioritizing his religious calling over professional sports opportunity. He established a family and business interests in Arizona while maintaining deep roots in the local LDS community where he had grown up.
delbert-l-stapley-1896.church_summary: Stapley served as a missionary in the Southern States Mission from 1915 to 1917. He was ordained as a member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles on October 5, 1950, and served in that capacity until his death on August 19, 1978. Throughout his apostolic career, Stapley was active in youth programs, receiving the Silver Buffalo Award from the Boy Scouts in 1969 for distinguished service. He was instrumental in organizing the original Miami Stake in 1961, bringing Church structure to rapidly growing communities in Florida. His service as an apostle spanned nearly three decades of significant growth and expansion in the Church.

dieter-f-uchtdorf-1940.life_summary: Dieter Friedrich Uchtdorf was born on November 6, 1940, in Moravská Ostrava (now Ostrava), Czechoslovakia, in the Nazi-occupied Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia. His early life was marked by the hardships of World War II and the subsequent communist regime in Eastern Europe. He developed a passion for aviation and became a commercial airline pilot, eventually serving as a captain with Lufthansa. Before his full-time church service, Uchtdorf built a successful career in aviation spanning decades, combining his professional expertise with his deep religious convictions. He married Harriet Reich on December 14, 1962, in the Swiss Temple, and the couple established their family while balancing his demanding airline career with active church participation.
dieter-f-uchtdorf-1940.church_summary: Uchtdorf served as an Area President and later held positions in the Presidency of the Seventy before his 2008 appointment to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles. He has emphasized themes of family relationships, eternal perspectives, the spiritual significance of women, and the principle of lifting where one stands. He dedicated nine temples across multiple continents, including facilities in Honduras, Guatemala, Brazil, Florida, Argentina, Peru, Mexico, Colorado, and Arizona. His ministry has been characterized by a focus on gracious acceptance of divine callings and teaching members to neither seek nor decline assignments given to them by church leaders.

ezra-taft-benson-1899.life_summary: Ezra Taft Benson was born August 4, 1899, in Whitney, Idaho, to a farming family in rural southeastern Idaho. He attended Brigham Young University, where he studied agricultural economics and developed expertise in farm management and rural development. Before his ecclesiastical career, Benson served as an agricultural economist and advisor, bringing practical knowledge of farming practices and rural life to his sphere of influence. He authored several publications on agricultural topics and maintained lifelong interest in farming and land stewardship. Benson was deeply engaged in secular economics and agricultural policy, serving the federal government as Secretary of Agriculture under President Eisenhower from 1953 to 1961, a position of national prominence.
ezra-taft-benson-1899.church_summary: Benson served as an LDS missionary in Britain from 1921 to 1923, where he was appointed president of the Newcastle Conference by David O. McKay. Ordained an apostle in 1943, he gained prominence as a Cold War voice in the church, emphasizing constitutional principles and individual liberty. He served as Secretary of Agriculture from 1953 to 1961 while maintaining apostolic duties. Upon becoming church president in 1985, Benson emphasized the Book of Mormon as central to LDS theology, launching a movement to read and study it intensively. His sermon on pride, drawing from C.S. Lewis's writings, became influential. He championed family, marriage, and personal moral agency as foundational gospel principles.

francis-m-lyman-1840.life_summary: Francis Marion Lyman was born in Illinois in 1840 and participated in the westward Mormon migration with his family, settling in Salt Lake Valley in 1848 at age eight. He helped drive livestock across the plains as part of the pioneer companies. Lyman came of age in the Utah Territory and developed skills in settlement leadership and political engagement. He presided over settlements in Fillmore and Tooele County, and gained recognition for his civic engagement, particularly for fighting government corruption during electoral disputes. His family legacy included both his father Amasa M. Lyman and his son Richard R. Lyman serving as apostles.
francis-m-lyman-1840.church_summary: Lyman was baptized at age eight and served two missions to England, with the first around 1860 and the second in 1873. His second mission expanded throughout Europe, visiting and proselytizing in Wales, Scotland, Denmark, Germany, Switzerland, and France. He was called to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and became president of that quorum in 1903. As an apostle, he conducted missionary work among Native Americans and oversaw the European Mission beginning in 1901. Lyman died of pneumonia in 1916, leaving a legacy of missionary service and ecclesiastical leadership.

franklin-d-richards-1821.life_summary: Franklin D. Richards (1821–1899) was an early LDS Church apostle who lived during the formative and expansion periods of the Church. Limited biographical information is available from standard sources, though he was the father of George F. Richards, who also became an apostle, and grandfather of LeGrand Richards. This three-generation succession of Richards family members in the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles represents one of the most remarkable family legacies in LDS Church history. His son George became the only person to serve as both Presiding Patriarch and President of the Quorum of the Twelve.
franklin-d-richards-1821.church_summary: Franklin D. Richards was called to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and served in that capacity during the mid-to-late nineteenth century. He died in 1899. His apostolic service occurred during a transformative period in Church history, and his family's continued prominence in leadership—with his son George and grandson LeGrand both achieving high positions—demonstrates the Richards family's enduring influence on institutional development. Limited details about his specific assignments and teachings are readily available in modern sources.

gary-e-stevenson-1955.life_summary: Gary Eugene Stevenson was born on August 6, 1955, in Ogden, Utah. He grew up in northern Utah and developed business acumen that led to a successful career in commerce and entrepreneurship. Before his full-time appointment in the Church's leadership, Stevenson built expertise in business operations and organizational management. He married Lesa Jean Higley in the Idaho Falls Idaho Temple, establishing a family partnership grounded in shared religious values. His professional accomplishments and business success prepared him for administrative responsibilities within Church governance while allowing him to bring practical experience from the private sector.
gary-e-stevenson-1955.church_summary: Stevenson served as a missionary in the Japan Fukuoka Mission during the mid-1970s, gaining cross-cultural experience and language skills. He later served as president of the Japan Nagano Mission from 2004 to 2007, demonstrating a sustained commitment to Japan and Japanese culture within the Church context. He was called to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 2015. His ministry has drawn on his business background to address Church organizational matters and administrative initiatives. His teachings and leadership style reflect an emphasis on efficient management and practical implementation of Church programs in diverse international settings.

george-a-smith-1817.life_summary: George Albert Smith was born June 26, 1817, in Potsdam, New York, the first cousin of Joseph Smith Jr. He joined the Church at age fifteen in 1832 and later moved to Ohio to meet his famous cousin for the first time. Smith grew to manhood as the religious movement expanded and faced persecution. He married eight women in his lifetime and fathered twenty children, establishing a large and influential family. Known for his distinctive personality, Smith earned a Paiute nickname meaning "takes himself apart" due to his habit of removing his wig and false teeth while preaching to audiences. He was known for his physical appearance and remarkable speaking style.
george-a-smith-1817.church_summary: George A. Smith became an ordained apostle in 1839 at age twenty-one. Following Joseph Smith's death, he pioneered westward with Brigham Young's 1847 expedition and helped establish Iron County, Utah, serving as its chief justice. From 1868 until his death in 1875, he served as First Counselor in the First Presidency to President Young. In August 1857, Smith toured southern Utah communities shortly before the Mountain Meadows Massacre; historical accounts suggest his tour, speeches, and personal actions contributed to fear and tension in these communities, though his exact role remains debated by scholars. He dedicated his life to establishing Mormon communities throughout southern Utah.

george-albert-smith-1870.life_summary: George Albert Smith was born on April 4, 1870, in Salt Lake City, Utah Territory, into a prominent LDS family as the son of John Henry Smith, an apostle, and Sarah Farr. He received his education in Salt Lake City schools and developed deep roots in the Utah community. Smith worked in various church-related endeavors while establishing himself as a devoted family man. He married Lucy Emily Woodruff, granddaughter of Church President Wilford Woodruff, on May 25, 1892, at the Manti Temple. The couple raised three children together until Lucy's death in 1937, after which Smith remained widowed for the remainder of his life. Known for his tireless dedication to church service, Smith traveled approximately a million miles throughout his ecclesiastical career.
george-albert-smith-1870.church_summary: George Albert Smith served a two-year Southern States Mission from 1892 to 1894, where he worked alongside J. Golden Kimball and served as mission secretary and acting mission president. He later presided over the British and European Mission from 1920 to 1921, preaching across the United Kingdom, Ireland, France, Netherlands, Switzerland, and Germany. Smith advanced through various church positions before becoming the eighth President of the LDS Church in 1945, serving until his death in 1951. He dedicated the Idaho Falls Temple on September 23, 1945. His ministry emphasized gospel authenticity, missionary revitalization, historical preservation, patriotic values, and youth development through church programs.
teaching_emphasis: Gospel authenticity and personal spiritual conviction
Youth development through MIA and Scout programs

george-f-richards-1861.life_summary: George Franklin Richards was born in Farmington, Utah Territory, in 1861 to Franklin D. Richards, himself an apostle. He came of age in a family tradition of Church leadership and followed his father into prominent ecclesiastical positions. Richards married Alice Robinson in 1882, with whom he had fifteen children. He was raised in the context of pioneer Utah and participated in the Church's institutional development throughout the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. His family became one of only three families in Church history with three consecutive generations serving in the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles—his father Franklin, himself George, and his son LeGrand.
george-f-richards-1861.church_summary: Richards was appointed to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles on April 9, 1906, and served until his death in 1950. He held unique and significant leadership positions: he served as president of the Salt Lake Temple from 1921 to 1938, was Acting Presiding Patriarch of the Church from 1937 to 1942, and became President of the Quorum of the Twelve from May 25, 1945, until his death. Remarkably, he remains the only person in Church history to have held both the offices of Presiding Patriarch and President of the Quorum of the Twelve. He also served as president of the European Mission beginning in 1916 and held a seat in the Utah House of Representatives.

george-q-cannon-1827.life_summary: George Quayle Cannon was born January 11, 1827, in Liverpool, England, to parents who were converted to the Latter-day Saint faith. His family immigrated to America when he was young, settling in the growing LDS communities in the Midwest and eventually moving west with the main body of the church. Cannon developed early aptitude in languages and printing, which became crucial to his later ecclesiastical responsibilities. He married Elizabeth Hoagland, with whom he had children, and in accordance with church doctrine practiced plural marriage, ultimately taking six wives and fathering thirty-three children who became prominent citizens and leaders in Utah and beyond. Cannon's education and talent for languages made him invaluable to the church's international missionary efforts.
george-q-cannon-1827.church_summary: Cannon was called to the apostleship on August 26, 1860, at age thirty-three, and immediately began serving in the First Presidency under four successive church presidents: Brigham Young, John Taylor, Wilford Woodruff, and Lorenzo Snow. He was the founding publisher and owner of The Juvenile Instructor magazine (1866), serving in that capacity until his death in 1901. He also served as the first general superintendent of the church's Sunday School from 1867 to 1901. Cannon held multiple significant church positions simultaneously: he was a five-time territorial delegate to the U.S. Congress (1872–1882), managing editor of the Deseret News (1867–1874), and an Oregon and California Mission President (1856–1858). He translated the Book of Mormon into Hawaiian, demonstrating his commitment to making scripture accessible to diverse peoples.
teaching_emphasis: Sunday School as primary teaching institution
Publishing and printing for religious purposes

george-q-morris-1874.life_summary: George Quincy Morris was born on February 20, 1874, in Salt Lake City, Utah Territory. He grew up in the center of LDS Church activity and received his education in Salt Lake Valley schools. Morris married Emma Ramsey on June 29, 1905, and together they had three daughters: Marian, Margery, and Helen. He established himself as a respected community leader and developed a reputation for sound judgment and spiritual maturity. Morris built a life that balanced family responsibilities with growing involvement in Church leadership at local and regional levels. His journey from lay member to Church leadership reflected his steady growth in spiritual authority and administrative capability over decades of faithful service.
george-q-morris-1874.church_summary: Morris served as a missionary in Great Britain from 1899 to 1902. He later served as Superintendent of the Young Men's Mutual Improvement Association (YMMIA) from 1937 to 1948, providing leadership for the Church's youth programs during a critical period. He was called as an Assistant to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 1951 and was ordained as a member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 1954. Morris made Church history by becoming the oldest person to be called to the apostleship, being ordained at the age of eighty. He served in the Quorum of the Twelve from 1954 until his death on April 23, 1962, eight years before his ninetieth birthday.
teaching_emphasis: Age is no barrier to spiritual growth

george-teasdale-1831.life_summary: George Teasdale was born in 1831 in England and embraced the gospel of Jesus Christ in his youth. He immigrated to America and made his home in Utah Territory, where he became deeply involved in the work of the Church. Like many British converts, Teasdale brought with him a strong educational background and commitment to community building. He lived during the era of intensive missionary work and was recognized for his ability to labor effectively in different parts of the world. His life embodied the dedication of early Church members who left their homes to build the kingdom.
george-teasdale-1831.church_summary: George Teasdale served as a dedicated missionary in multiple locations, including Mexico, and was ordained as an apostle in the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles. He devoted his life to missionary work and ecclesiastical service, demonstrating consistent commitment to advancing the Church's growth. His service spanned the period of significant institutional development and he participated in key Church councils and decisions of his era. He died in 1907 at an advanced age, having spent decades in Church leadership.

gerald-causse-1963.life_summary: Gérald Caussé was born on May 20, 1963, in Bordeaux, France, where he grew up in a French-speaking environment. He obtained a Master's degree in business from ESSEC Business School, an elite institution in France, which prepared him for leadership roles in organizational management and finance. Before his full-time church service, Caussé served in the French Air Force for one year. He married Valérie Lucienne Babin on August 5, 1986, in the Bern Switzerland Temple, and together they raised five children. Beyond his church responsibilities, Caussé demonstrated creative talents as a musician, collaborating with composer Nicolas Giusti to produce three piano albums: Joyful (2019), Noël (2020), and As a Child (2023).
gerald-causse-1963.church_summary: Caussé was called as a member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles on November 6, 2025, and accepted as a prophet, seer, and revelator according to church doctrine. He has been instrumental in expanding the Church's humanitarian initiatives, increasing charitable giving to nearly $1 billion annually under his leadership. His ministry emphasizes compassionate service and faithful stewardship of church resources, drawing on his business education and organizational experience to strengthen the global impact of the Latter-day Saint movement.

gerrit-w-gong-1953.life_summary: Gerrit Wessel Gong was born on December 23, 1953, in Redwood City, California. He grew up in California during the mid-twentieth century and pursued advanced education in international relations and East Asian studies. Before his appointment to Church leadership, Gong established himself as a scholar and academic, earning advanced degrees and conducting research on East Asian geopolitics, Sino-Japanese relations, and international diplomacy. His scholarly work focused on Taiwan Strait policy, the Korean Peninsula, and U.S.-China relations. On January 4, 1980, he married Susan Lindsay, daughter of Richard P. Lindsay, at the Salt Lake Temple, and the couple established their family while he continued his academic pursuits and Church service.
gerrit-w-gong-1953.church_summary: Gong served as a missionary in Taiwan during his youth, gaining fluency in Mandarin Chinese and deep cultural understanding of East Asia. He was called to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 2018, becoming the second member of Asian descent to serve in this position. He has presided over temple dedications and groundbreakings, including the Winnipeg Manitoba Temple dedication in November 2020 and the Taylorsville Utah Temple groundbreaking in October 2020. His unique background in international relations and East Asian culture has positioned him to lead the Church's expansion in Asia and foster dialogue between the Church and East Asian communities, bringing scholarly insight to theological matters.
teaching_emphasis: East Asian culture and international relations
Standards of civilization in international society

gordon-b-hinckley-1910.life_summary: Gordon Bitner Hinckley was born June 23, 1910, in Salt Lake City, Utah, to a prominent church and business family. His father, Bryant S. Hinckley, was a successful businessman and church leader, providing Gordon with a cultured, educated family environment. Hinckley attended the University of Utah and later studied at Oxford University as a visiting student, bringing international educational experience to his formation. Before his full-time ecclesiastical service, he worked in business and public relations, including employment with the church's public communications office. He developed exceptional skills in public speaking, writing, and media relations that would distinguish his later ecclesiastical career. Hinckley earned respect as an articulate, forward-thinking communicator across secular and religious spheres.
gordon-b-hinckley-1910.church_summary: Hinckley served as an LDS missionary in the British Mission (1933–1935) from London. Ordained an apostle in 1961, he advanced through leadership positions including counselor to church presidents. He became church president in 1995 and led until his death in 2008, serving nearly thirteen years. During his presidency, Hinckley dedicated or rededicated 92 temples overall, with 65 additional dedications and five rededications as president, dramatically expanding the church's temple network. He authored 'The Family: A Proclamation to the World' (1995), a foundational statement on family values. Hinckley championed the Perpetual Education Fund (2001) to assist members in developing nations, education accessibility, humanitarian aid, and six personal virtues: gratitude, intelligence, cleanliness, honesty, humility, and prayerfulness.
temples_dedicated: Multiple temples (92 total dedicated or rededicated)
teaching_emphasis: Six virtues: gratitude, intelligence, cleanliness, honesty, humility, prayerfulness

harold-b-lee-1899.life_summary: Harold Bingham Lee was born March 28, 1899, in Clifton, Idaho, to farming and railroad families in rural southeastern Idaho. He attended local schools and later brigham Young Academy, where he excelled in his studies and demonstrated early leadership ability. Lee worked as a teacher before his church service, developing skills in communication and instruction. He earned respect as a young educator in Idaho communities and brought practical experience in reaching and influencing youth. Lee's background in small-town Utah-Idaho culture and education shaped his later emphasis on youth development and personal spiritual responsibility. His upbringing in a tight-knit agricultural community fostered values of service and community orientation.
harold-b-lee-1899.church_summary: Lee served a western states mission with headquarters in Denver, Colorado, from 1920 to 1922. Called to the quorum of seventy and later ordained an apostle in 1941, he gained prominence for innovative work with youth organizations and seminary programs. He published influential books on spiritual living including 'Youth and the Church' and 'Stand Ye in Holy Places.' Lee became counselor to church presidents and was sustained as president in 1972, serving a brief tenure of nearly two years. His ministry stressed personal spiritual responsibility, priesthood correlation, and the spiritual foundations of individual and family life. He died December 26, 1973, from a pulmonary hemorrhage.

hb-eyring-1933.life_summary: Henry Bennion Eyring was born on May 31, 1933, in Princeton, New Jersey, to a prominent family with connections to the LDS Church. Growing up in New Jersey provided him with exposure to the northeastern United States and a diverse cultural environment. Eyring received his education through university studies and developed interests in science, mathematics, and technology. He married Kathleen Johnson on July 27, 1962, at the LDS Church's Logan Temple, beginning a marriage that lasted 61 years until Kathleen's death on October 15, 2023. The couple built their life together while Eyring balanced scientific and professional pursuits with deep ecclesiastical commitments. Eyring's background in technology and analysis, combined with his spiritual conviction, made him a unique voice in modern church leadership.
hb-eyring-1933.church_summary: Henry B. Eyring served as a district missionary for the LDS Church while stationed at Sandia Base in New Mexico during his Air Force service, where he also worked analyzing weapons test data. He was later called to positions of increasing responsibility within church leadership, eventually being called to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles. Eyring has dedicated multiple temples including San Salvador El Salvador, Gilbert Arizona, Payson Utah, Indianapolis Indiana, and Philadelphia Pennsylvania. He also rededicated the Buenos Aires Argentina and Mexico City Mexico Temples. His published works emphasize faith, covenants, leadership, spiritual gifts, family, truth-seeking, and moral development. His teaching spans theological and practical dimensions, including works such as 'A Life Founded in Light and Truth' and 'Teaching Is a Moral Act.'

heber-c-kimball-1801.life_summary: Heber Chase Kimball was born on June 14, 1801, in Sheldon, Franklin County, Vermont. He grew up in rural New England during the early nineteenth century and developed practical skills in farming and craftsmanship. Before joining the LDS Church, Kimball was involved in various occupations and trades. He married his first wife, Vilate Murray, in November 1822, and the couple established a family together. Following his conversion to the LDS faith, Kimball became a devoted adherent and eventually one of the church's most prominent leaders. Throughout his life, Kimball married a total of 43 women and fathered 66 children by 17 of his wives, reflecting his complete commitment to the church's doctrine of plural marriage. His polygamist family became one of the largest and most prominent in early LDS history.
heber-c-kimball-1801.church_summary: Heber C. Kimball served eight missions between 1832 and 1840, with his most significant missionary work occurring in England from 1837 to 1838, when he led a missionary group that established the church's first English proselyting effort in Preston, Lancashire. His first mission resulted in approximately 1,500 baptisms before his departure for the United States in 1838. He served a second England mission from 1839 to 1841, working in Preston and London. Kimball was ordained an apostle and became a key counselor to church leadership. He served as First Counselor in the Presidency under Brigham Young and was deeply involved in the development of early Utah communities. His ministry emphasized obedience to divine instruction and the building of economically independent communities.

heber-j-grant-1856.life_summary: Heber J. Grant was born November 22, 1856, in Salt Lake City, Utah Territory, to wealthy, prominent church leaders. His father, Jedediah M. Grant, died when Heber was an infant, leaving him raised by his mother in relative affluence. Grant received education at the University of Deseret and developed business acumen, becoming a skilled investor and entrepreneur. He engaged in banking, mining, and ranching ventures, achieving considerable wealth and business reputation in Utah Territory. Grant also pursued musical interests and served in military capacities during territorial conflicts. His secular success demonstrated that religious devotion and commercial enterprise could flourish together.
heber-j-grant-1856.church_summary: Grant served missions to Native Americans (1883–1884), to the Yaqui in Mexico, and as mission president to Japan (1901–1903) and Britain and Europe (1903–1906). Ordained an apostle in 1882, he became counselor to church presidents and eventually church president in 1918, leading until his death in 1945. Grant championed seminary and institute education, emphasized Word of Wisdom adherence, and established the welfare program emphasizing self-sufficiency and dignity. He dedicated the Arizona and Hawaii temples and oversaw temple expansion. His presidency stressed institutional efficiency, education, and social responsibility.

henry-d-moyle-1889.life_summary: Henry Dinwoodey Moyle was born on April 22, 1889, in Salt Lake City, Utah Territory. He grew up in the urban center of the LDS Church and received his education in Salt Lake Valley schools. Moyle married Clara Alberta Wright on a date in the early twentieth century at the Salt Lake Temple, and together they had six children. He established himself as a respected community and Church figure, bringing professional acumen to ecclesiastical responsibilities. His career spanned the transformative decades of the twentieth century, from the early years after statehood through the post-World War II era. Moyle's life was characterized by a willingness to experiment with innovative approaches to Church growth and membership engagement.
henry-d-moyle-1889.church_summary: Moyle served as a missionary in Switzerland and Germany during his youth. He was ordained to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 1947 and served in that capacity until his death in 1963. During his apostolic ministry, Moyle became known for implementing innovative but ultimately controversial initiatives aimed at increasing Church membership and engagement. Most notably, he developed the baseball baptism program, designed to attract converts through athletic engagement, though this approach was largely opposed by other apostles and proved unsuccessful in retaining active members. Despite the mixed reception of some initiatives, Moyle remained committed to the task of strengthening the Church.

howard-w-hunter-1907.life_summary: Howard William Hunter was born November 14, 1907, in Boise, Idaho, to a business and professional family. He was educated at Brigham Young University and received training in business and accounting, becoming a certified public accountant. Hunter enjoyed music and played the violin, maintaining artistic pursuits throughout his life. He established himself as a respected accountant and businessman in California, where he spent much of his career before his ecclesiastical service became his primary focus. Hunter served in business and professional capacities in Los Angeles and maintained a reputation for integrity and careful financial management. He balanced commercial success with significant church service, demonstrating that secular achievement and religious commitment could coexist.
howard-w-hunter-1907.church_summary: Hunter served a mission location not specifically documented in available sources. Ordained an apostle in 1959, he became known for his diplomatic approach, reconciliation efforts, and emphasis on Christ-like living and temple attendance. He served as president of the Los Angeles Temple and later as president of the Oakland Temple. As church president from June 1994 until his death in March 1995, Hunter served the shortest presidency in church history at nine months. During his brief tenure, he prioritized temple attendance and Christ-centered discipleship. He dedicated the Bountiful Utah Temple, the Orlando Florida Temple, and presided at the dedication of the BYU Jerusalem Center. His emphasis on reconciliation and invitation to return to church became defining themes.

hugh-b-brown-1883.life_summary: Hugh Bennion Brown was born on October 24, 1883, in Granger, Utah Territory. He grew up in the rural communities of early Utah and received his foundational education in territorial schools. Brown married Zina Young Card in 1908, and together they had eight children, building a substantial family. Before his prominence in Church leadership, Brown pursued professional and civic responsibilities, including work in Canada where he established significant business and community interests. He was known for his intellectual curiosity, sense of humor, and willingness to engage with new ideas. His life reflected a commitment to personal growth and intellectual vigor alongside steadfast religious conviction.
hugh-b-brown-1883.church_summary: Brown served as a missionary in England from 1904 to 1906 under the direction of Heber J. Grant. He became president of the Lethbridge, Alberta Stake in 1921 and served as president of the British Mission in two separate periods (1937–1940 and 1944–1946). During World War II, he served as LDS Servicemen's Coordinator (1941–1945), providing pastoral care to Church members in military service. He was called as an Assistant to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 1953 and ordained as a member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 1958. From 1961 to 1970, he served as First Counselor in the First Presidency, providing leadership alongside Church president David O. McKay.

hyrum-mack-smith-1872.life_summary: Hyrum Mack Smith was born March 21, 1872, in Salt Lake City, Utah Territory, to Joseph F. Smith and Edna Lambson. He was the eldest son in his family and inherited a legacy of church leadership through his father, who would become church president. His paternal grandfather was Hyrum Smith, the brother of LDS founder Joseph Smith, connecting him directly to the founding generation. Smith graduated from Latter-day Saint College in 1894. On November 15, 1895, he married Ida Elizabeth Bowman and subsequently served a two-year mission in Great Britain, presiding over the Newcastle Conference from 1896 to 1898. He and Ida had five children together, though family life was marked by tragedy.
hyrum-mack-smith-1872.church_summary: Hyrum Mack Smith was ordained as an apostle on October 24, 1901, at age twenty-nine by his father, Joseph F. Smith. In 1909, he became one of two original priesthood advisors to the Primary Association, helping shape the religious education of the Church's children. From 1913 to 1916, he served as president of the European Mission until World War I suspended activities. He died January 23, 1918, at age forty-five from a ruptured appendix. His wife Ida died from childbirth complications in September 1918 while pregnant with their fifth child. His descendants continued to serve prominently in the Church, including his son Joseph Fielding Smith, who became presiding patriarch.
hyrum-mack-smith-1872.birth_place: Salt Lake City, Utah Territory, United States
hyrum-mack-smith-1872.death_place: Salt Lake City, Utah, United States

hyrum-smith-1800.life_summary: Hyrum Smith was born February 9, 1800, in Tunbridge, Vermont, to Joseph Smith Sr. and Lucy Mack Smith. He was the eldest brother of Joseph Smith Jr. and grew up in a family of modest means. Between ages twelve and fifteen, Hyrum attended Moor's Charity School on the campus of Dartmouth College in Lebanon, New Hampshire, gaining education unusual for his social class. He was baptized in 1829 and became one of the Eight Witnesses, testifying to the reality of the golden plates. Hyrum married and had eight children, establishing himself as a committed member of his brother's new religious movement. His combination of family loyalty, spiritual commitment, and ecclesiastical responsibility made him one of Joseph's closest and most trusted advisors throughout the founder's ministry.
hyrum-smith-1800.church_summary: Hyrum Smith was baptized in 1829 and became one of the Eight Witnesses to the Book of Mormon plates. When the church formally organized in 1830, he was the oldest charter member at age thirty. He served as a branch presiding officer and missionary, later becoming the church's Presiding Patriarch and Assistant President of the Church. Hyrum traveled with Joseph to Carthage, Illinois, in 1844 to face riot and treason charges. On June 27, 1844, during a mob attack on the jail, Hyrum was shot in the face and then struck again, declaring "I am a dead man" before his death. By 2000, estimates suggested over thirty-one thousand living descendants from his line.

j-reuben-clark-1871.life_summary: Joshua Reuben Clark Jr. was born September 1, 1871, in Grantsville, Utah Territory, to parents of English and Swiss descent. A voracious student and ambitious intellectual, he excelled academically at the University of Utah before pursuing advanced legal training at Columbia University Law School. His distinguished career in international diplomacy included service as Assistant Solicitor and Solicitor in the U.S. State Department, Under-Secretary of State under President Calvin Coolidge, and U.S. Ambassador to Mexico (1930–1933). Clark authored the influential Clark Memorandum, which reinterpreted the Monroe Doctrine and established him as a major figure in twentieth-century American foreign policy. He navigated elite academic, diplomatic, and governmental circles with distinction before redirecting his energies toward full-time Church service.
j-reuben-clark-1871.church_summary: In 1933, Clark was called to the First Presidency as Second Counselor to President Heber J. Grant and was ordained an apostle in 1934. He served as Second Counselor under George Albert Smith (1945–1951) and as First Counselor under David O. McKay (1951–1959, 1959–1961), accumulating over 28 years of service in the Church's highest councils. His presidency focused on character-building through welfare initiatives and defending the Church's institutional independence from state interference. His published works, including Our Lord of the Gospels and Why the King James Version, reflected his intellectual rigor and spiritual depth. He modeled the integration of worldly expertise and ecclesiastical authority, demonstrating that the Church could benefit from leaders educated in secular excellence.
teaching_emphasis: Legal and constitutional defense of Church interests

james-e-faust-1920.life_summary: James Esdras Faust was born on July 31, 1920, in Delta, Utah, a small town in west-central Utah. He married Ruth Wright on April 21, 1943, and together they had five children: James Hamilton, Janna R. Coombs, Marcus G., Lisa A. Smith, and Robert P. Faust. Ruth was his steadfast companion throughout his life and ministry until her death on February 10, 2008, just months after his own. Faust developed a reputation as a bridge-builder within the church and served in various capacities that drew on his legal expertise and diplomatic sensibilities, earning him respect from both church members and civic leaders.
james-e-faust-1920.church_summary: Faust served as a missionary in southern Brazil from 1939 to 1942, beginning his church service during the Depression era. He rose through the church hierarchy to become a member of the First Presidency alongside Gordon B. Hinckley and Thomas S. Monson, with whom he constituted the longest continuously serving First Presidency in LDS Church history. As area president in Brazil, Faust helped establish the São Paulo Brazil Temple. He was notably the first LDS apostle to travel to Nigeria in early 1979, where he baptized five men. Faust's ministry emphasized finding light in a dark world, spiritual gifts, personal narratives, and reaching upward for divine guidance. He died on August 10, 2007.

james-e-talmage-1862.life_summary: James Edward Talmage was born September 21, 1862, in Hungerford, Berkshire, England, to a cultivated family that valued both spiritual conviction and scientific knowledge. He emigrated to Utah as a boy and distinguished himself in advanced studies, earning credentials in geology, chemistry, and mining engineering. Talmage worked as a mining consultant and university educator, establishing himself as an expert in applied chemistry and geological science. His academic career included presidencies of Brigham Young Academy and the University of Utah (1893–1897), where he pioneered the integration of rigorous scientific training with religious education. He possessed an uncommon ability to navigate the tension between evolutionary thinking and revealed doctrine, advocating for harmonization rather than conflict.
james-e-talmage-1862.church_summary: Talmage served as president of the Church's European Mission from 1924 to 1928 and was ordained to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 1911, serving until his death in 1933. He authored two foundational theological works—Jesus the Christ and Articles of Faith—which became standard references for LDS doctrine and biblical interpretation.
