His teaching emphasized the compatibility of scientific discovery with religious truth, famously stating that the Gospel contains room for all true knowledge. He lectured extensively on Church history, doctrine, and the evidence for Latter-day Saint claims, becoming the Church's preeminent voice for intellectual and spiritual reconciliation.

jedediah-m-grant-1816.life_summary: Jedediah Morgan Grant was born February 21, 1816, in Windsor, New York, to a family of moderate means. In his youth, he received practical education in farming and trade skills common to rural northeastern communities. Grant converted to Mormonism in the 1830s and relocated to Ohio, then Missouri with the church. He became a forceful personality in the growing Mormon communities, gaining reputation as a stirring public speaker and community organizer. Before his death, Grant was regarded as a rising church leader with influence over younger members and significant respect for his dynamic personality and rhetorical abilities.
jedediah-m-grant-1816.church_summary: Grant served early missions to the eastern United States, including Maryland, North Carolina, Virginia, and New Jersey, where he directed missionary work and gained converts. Called as a counselor to Brigham Young, Grant became a principal leader of Utah Territory in its early years. In 1856, he launched the Mormon Reformation, a movement calling members to rebaptism and renewed religious commitment through intense preaching. Known as 'Brigham's Sledgehammer' for his forceful oratory, Grant delivered fiery sermons emphasizing repentance and covenant renewal. He died unexpectedly in December 1856 from pneumonia, cutting short a promising ecclesiastical career.

jeffrey-r-holland-1940.life_summary: Jeffrey Roy Holland was born on December 3, 1940, and became an accomplished educator and scholar before his religious leadership. He earned a bachelor's degree in English from Brigham Young University and pursued advanced degrees, including master's degrees in religious education and American studies, and a PhD from Yale University. Holland held several significant academic positions throughout his career, serving as BYU's ninth president from 1980 to 1989. During his BYU tenure, he established the Jerusalem Center and emphasized academic excellence within a faith-based environment. He also oversaw the successful Excellence in the Eighties fundraising campaign. Holland married Patricia Terry in 1963 and had three children with her.
jeffrey-r-holland-1940.church_summary: Holland served as commissioner of the Church Educational System from 1976 to 1980 before his appointment as a general authority of the LDS Church. He was ordained as an apostle in 1994 and became a general authority seventy. In 2023, he assumed the role of acting president of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, and in October 2025, he became president of the Quorum following Jeffrey R. Holland's appointment. Holland's wife Patricia Terry Holland passed away in July 2023. He died on December 27, 2025, from kidney disease complications in Salt Lake City at age 85.
jeffrey-r-holland-1940.death_place: Salt Lake City, Utah, United States

john-a-widtsoe-1872.life_summary: John Andreas Widtsoe was born January 31, 1872, on Frøya Island in Sør-Trøndelag, Norway, to parents who embraced Mormonism before emigrating to Utah. Raised in a frontier community but exposed to European intellectual traditions through his parents, Widtsoe developed a passion for scientific inquiry and religious understanding. He distinguished himself through agricultural studies and research at Utah State Agricultural College, where he eventually became president (1907–1916). His academic career demonstrated the value of applying scientific method to solving agricultural problems affecting Utah farmers. Before his ecclesiastical service, he had established himself as a university president and educational innovator, bridging agricultural science and rural Mormon communities.
john-a-widtsoe-1872.church_summary: Widtsoe was ordained to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 1921 and served until his death in 1952. He also served as Commissioner of Church Education (1921–1924, 1934–1936) and as European Mission President (1926–1932), where he dedicated Czechoslovakia and other Eastern European nations for missionary work. His authored works, including Evidences and Reconciliations and A Rational Theology, addressed questions of faith and science while acknowledging diverse interpretations available to Latter-day Saints. He brought intellectual rigor to apologetics and established frameworks for Mormon thinkers to engage modern scholarship without abandoning their convictions.

john-e-page-1799.life_summary: John E. Page was born in 1799 in the northeastern United States during a period of religious ferment and revival. Little is definitively documented about his early life and secular pursuits prior to joining the Latter-day Saint movement. Page came of age during an era of westward expansion and participated in various settlement efforts. He was married multiple times as polygamy became doctrine within the church. Page worked as a lay preacher and missionary, traveling extensively to spread the gospel message. His life was marked by the tumultuous events of early church history, including conflicts in Missouri and Illinois.
john-e-page-1799.church_summary: Page was an early convert to the LDS Church and served as an apostle, though records of his exact tenure and contributions are less detailed than those of some of his contemporaries. He participated in various missionary missions and was involved in church settlement projects. Page's ministry took place during the foundational era of the church when institutional structures were still being developed and major theological doctrines were being established. He remained involved in church activities throughout the early period of Latter-day Saint history, though documentation of specific callings and accomplishments is limited in readily available sources.

john-f-boynton-1811.life_summary: John F. Boynton was born on September 20, 1811, in Bradford, Massachusetts, in New England's heart. He grew up during a period of intense American religious revival and westward expansion. Boynton married Susan Lowell early in his life, though few details of this union are recorded. He was an active and itinerant minister during the 1830s, traveling extensively throughout the northeastern United States and Canada. Late in life, after his apostolic service had ended, he married Mary West Jenkins in 1865. Boynton lived a long life spanning nearly eighty years, witnessing the transformation of America from a young republic into an industrial nation.
john-f-boynton-1811.church_summary: Boynton was ordained an elder by Sidney Rigdon and quickly engaged in intensive missionary work. In 1832, he served in Erie County, Pennsylvania, with Zebedee Coltrin, and from December 1832 onwards labored in Maine, where he baptized approximately forty individuals and, in partnership with Elder Even M. Greene, brought approximately 130 converts into the church. He was called to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles on February 15, 1835, and participated in a mission to the eastern United States and Upper Canada in June 1835. However, his apostolic career was brief; he was excommunicated on December 3, 1837. After leaving the church, Boynton relocated to New York, where he lived out his remaining years.

john-henry-smith-1848.life_summary: John Henry Smith was born September 19, 1848, in Salt Lake City, Utah Territory, to apostle George A. Smith. He grew to manhood in a prominent church family, inheriting both spiritual responsibility and civic engagement. Smith received education appropriate to his station and participated in the early development of Utah Territory. He married and fathered nineteen children through plural marriage, establishing a large and influential family. Smith was known for his integrity and his ability to bridge ecclesiastical and political spheres. He died of pulmonary hemorrhage in Salt Lake City, having witnessed and participated in many of the transformative events of Utah's territorial period.
john-henry-smith-1848.church_summary: John Henry Smith held various positions within the LDS Church beginning in 1867. He served as a European missionary in 1874–1875, primarily in England, spreading Church influence during a significant period of international expansion. In October 1880, Church president John Taylor called Smith to be a member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles. Following the death of John R. Winder, he joined the First Presidency in 1910, serving as counselor to the Church president. Smith served alongside his father George A. Smith in the Quorum of the Twelve from 1903 to 1910, making them one of the few father-son pairs to serve together in that governing body.
john-henry-smith-1848.birth_place: Salt Lake City, Utah Territory, United States
john-henry-smith-1848.death_place: Salt Lake City, Utah, United States

john-smith-1781.life_summary: John Smith was born in 1781 and served in important roles within the early Latter Day Saint movement. He was the uncle of Joseph Smith Jr., providing family connections to the founder and representing the broader Smith family's involvement in the religious movement. As part of the extended Smith clan, he was present during the organization and expansion of the Church. He lived during the early period of westward expansion and settlement, witnessing the transformation of the movement from a small New England group to a significant religious organization.
john-smith-1781.church_summary: John Smith served as Presiding Patriarch and member of the First Presidency of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. His ecclesiastical roles placed him among the highest leadership of the early Church, where he participated in administrative and patriarchal functions. He provided spiritual guidance to church members as Presiding Patriarch and represented the church in its governing councils.

john-taylor-1808.life_summary: John Taylor was born on November 1, 1808, in Milnthorpe, Westmorland, in the Lake District of England, a region of rural beauty and Methodist religious influence. He grew up in a time of significant social upheaval in Britain, witnessing the Industrial Revolution and its profound effects on English society. Taylor received education befitting a merchant-class family and developed intellectual and spiritual capacities that would later mark his leadership. On January 28, 1833, he married Leonora Cannon. As his life unfolded, Taylor would practice plural marriage, eventually taking eight wives—Leonora Cannon, Elizabeth Kaighin, Jane Ballantyne, Mary Ann Oakley, Sophia Whitaker, Harriet Whitaker, Margaret Young, and Josephine Elizabeth Roueche—and fathering thirty-four children across these unions.
john-taylor-1808.church_summary: Taylor served in multiple important missionary roles, beginning with the France Mission in 1849, where he became the first Latter-day Saint mission president in France and published the newspaper L'Etoile du Deseret (Star of Deseret). He also served on the Eastern States Mission, based in New York City, and on the Britain Mission in 1839, where he preached throughout Liverpool, Ireland, and the Isle of Man. Rising through church leadership, Taylor eventually became Church President and during his tenure canonized the Pearl of Great Price in October 1880 and oversaw significant expansion of church hierarchy and the establishment of Mormon colonies across multiple territories. His teaching and leadership centered on defending plural marriage against increasing government opposition and on coordinating economic development through institutions like Zion's Central Board of Trade, seeking to create a comprehensive Latter-day Saint community and civilization.
john-taylor-1808.burial_place: Salt Lake City Cemetery, Salt Lake City, Utah, United States

john-w-taylor-1858.life_summary: John Wentworth Taylor was born on May 15, 1858, in Provo, Utah Territory, the son of John Taylor, the third president of the Latter-day Saint Church. Growing up in a prominent Church family gave him unique access to leadership circles and theological instruction. John W. Taylor received his early education at Deseret University and later worked in various civic and journalistic capacities in Idaho. As a young man, he served as county clerk and newspaper editor in Cassia County, Idaho, combining his family's intellectual legacy with practical community service. He married multiple times in accordance with Church doctrine of his era, eventually having six wives and fathering thirty-six children.
john-w-taylor-1858.church_summary: John W. Taylor was ordained a deacon circa 1872 and a teacher in 1874. He was ordained an apostle on April 9, 1884, at age 26, becoming one of the youngest apostles in Church history. Serving in the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, he conducted missionary work in the United States, Canada, and England. However, his adherence to plural marriage after the 1890 Manifesto created tension with Church leadership. He resigned from the Quorum on October 28, 1905, and was excommunicated on March 28, 1911. He was posthumously rebaptized and reinstated on May 21, 1965. He died on October 10, 1916, from stomach cancer.
john-w-taylor-1858.death_place: Forest Dale, Salt Lake County, Utah, United States
john-w-taylor-1858.burial_place: Salt Lake City Cemetery, Salt Lake City, Utah

john-willard-young-1844.life_summary: John Willard Young was born on October 1, 1844, in Nauvoo, Illinois, the fifth son of Brigham Young, who would become the second president of the LDS Church and the colonizer of the Great Basin. Young grew up in a household of extraordinary influence and privilege during the turbulent early migration years of the Latter-day Saint movement. As an adult, Young spent much of his life engaged in business ventures, establishing himself as an entrepreneur in the East rather than remaining in Salt Lake City. He eventually settled in New York City, where he pursued commercial and financial interests, maintaining nominal ecclesiastical status while devoting himself primarily to secular enterprises.
john-willard-young-1844.church_summary: Young held significant ecclesiastical positions including counselor in the First Presidency and apostle, though these roles occupied less of his attention than his business pursuits. He lived much of his adult life in New York City rather than at church headquarters, creating a notable distance between his ecclesiastical status and active participation. Young's tenure saw changes to church succession policy and apostolic responsibilities. Despite his prestigious lineage and prominent ecclesiastical assignments, Young's ministry was marked more by administrative function than by documented spiritual teaching or theological contribution. He died on February 12, 1924, in New York City, ending a life that reflected the tension between ecclesiastical privilege and secular ambition.
john-willard-young-1844.death_place: New York City, New York, USA

joseph-b-wirthlin-1917.life_summary: Joseph Bitner Wirthlin was born on June 11, 1917, in Salt Lake City, Utah, to a family with long-standing prominence in the LDS Church. He married Elisa Young Rogers on May 26, 1941, in the Salt Lake Temple, and they had eight children together. Elisa died in August 2006 of causes incident to age, after more than sixty-five years of marriage. Wirthlin established himself as a thoughtful leader with a distinctive approach to spiritual teaching, notably using sports analogies and examples to explain matters of faith. His tenure in leadership extended into the late twentieth century, making him a bridge figure between different eras of church administration.
joseph-b-wirthlin-1917.church_summary: Wirthlin served as a missionary in Germany, Austria, and Switzerland from 1936 to 1939, during the turbulent pre-World War II period in Europe. He was ordained an apostle in 1986 and served in the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles until his death on December 1, 2008. Before his apostolic appointment, Wirthlin served as president of the Europe Area from 1984, bringing his experience and stability to a region experiencing significant church growth. At the time of his death, he was the oldest apostle among the ranks of the church. Wirthlin's distinctive teaching style, which employed sports to explain faith and spiritual principles, made his messages particularly accessible and memorable to diverse audiences.

joseph-f-merrill-1868.life_summary: Joseph Franklin Merrill was born in 1868 and rose to prominence as an educator and religious administrator within the LDS Church. He developed expertise in educational curriculum design and the administration of Church educational institutions. Before his elevation to apostolic office, Merrill served in various capacities within the Church's education system, including leadership of the Deseret Normal School (later Utah State University). His career reflected the Church's increasing investment in formal education as a means of preserving and transmitting Mormon identity. He brought both practical educational expertise and deep theological commitment to his work in the emerging field of religious education.
joseph-f-merrill-1868.church_summary: Merrill was ordained an apostle in 1931 and served in the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles until his death in 1952. He oversaw the Church's educational mission at a crucial period when secondary and higher education became integral to Mormon institutional life. His work as a mission president and in various ecclesiastical capacities demonstrated his ability to inspire others toward educational excellence and spiritual commitment. He emphasized the compatibility of rigorous secular learning with faithful religious practice, positioning Mormon education as distinctly modern while theologically grounded in restoration principles.
teaching_emphasis: Science and learning within faith frameworks

joseph-f-smith-1838.life_summary: Joseph Fielding Smith Sr. was born November 13, 1838, in Far West, Missouri, to Hyrum Smith and Mary Fielding Smith. He experienced significant hardship in childhood, as his father Hyrum was imprisoned under Missouri's extermination order shortly before his birth. After his father's execution in 1844, his mother Mary Fielding raised both her biological children and Hyrum's six children from his first marriage. Smith's mother died in 1852, leaving him an orphan at thirteen. As a young boy of seven, Smith drove oxen teams to Winter Quarters, Nebraska, during the westward exodus. Despite these hardships, he developed into a capable leader and administrator.
joseph-f-smith-1838.church_summary: Joseph F. Smith undertook multiple missionary assignments beginning at age fifteen to the Sandwich Islands. He served in Hawaii, England, and conducted various other assignments for the Church. Church leaders recognized his abilities, and he was ordained an apostle by Brigham Young in 1866. Smith became church president in 1901 and served until his death in 1918. He addressed the challenge of ongoing polygamous practices by issuing the "second manifesto" in 1904, declaring that church members performing plural marriages would face excommunication. Smith made substantial doctrinal contributions, including statements on evolution, the nature of God, and spiritual redemption. He died from pneumonia during the 1918 influenza pandemic, becoming the last LDS Church president who had personally known Joseph Smith Jr.

joseph-fielding-smith-1876.life_summary: Joseph Fielding Smith Jr. was born July 19, 1876, in Salt Lake City to Joseph F. Smith, who would later become church president. He grew to manhood in a family of prominence and responsibility within the LDS Church. Smith received education appropriate to his position and family status. He married three times during his lifetime: first to Louie Emily Shurtliff, who died in 1908; then to Ethel Georgina Reynolds, who died in 1937; and finally to Jessie Ella Evans in 1938. His marriages produced a substantial family, and he was a devoted husband and father despite the losses he experienced in widowhood.
joseph-fielding-smith-1876.church_summary: Joseph Fielding Smith Jr. was named to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 1910 at age thirty-four. He later served as Church Historian and Recorder, a position he held for nearly fifty years, making him one of the Church's primary custodians of historical records and doctrinal archives. Smith was a prolific author, publishing twenty-five books on religious subjects. He served as President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles from 1951 to 1970, ranking as the third-longest tenure in that position. Smith held rigid orthodoxy in his theological views, particularly opposing evolutionary theory, and authored Man, His Origin and Destiny to challenge evolution, though church leadership did not officially endorse this work. He became the tenth president of the Church in 1970 at age ninety-three, making him the oldest person to assume that office. His brief presidency introduced area conferences, organizational reforms, and temple dedications in Ogden and Provo. He died peacefully at home on July 2, 1972.
joseph-fielding-smith-1876.birth_place: Salt Lake City, Utah, United States

joseph-smith-jr-1805.life_summary: Joseph Smith Jr. was born December 23, 1805, in Sharon, Vermont, during a period of intense religious ferment known as the Second Great Awakening. His family struggled financially throughout his youth, moving frequently in search of economic opportunity. Smith received limited formal education but displayed early inclination toward spiritual matters and folk traditions. In 1823, he claimed to have received a vision of an angel named Moroni, beginning a series of revelatory experiences that would define his life. He grew to manhood in western New York, where he worked as a farm laborer and treasure seeker before his religious calling transformed him into one of America's most influential religious founders.
joseph-smith-jr-1805.church_summary: Smith founded the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in 1830 at age twenty-four, publishing the Book of Mormon and claiming authority as prophet and president of the Church. He established settlements in Ohio, Missouri, and Illinois, serving as prophet, presiding officer, and theological innovator throughout his ministry. He introduced controversial doctrines including polygamy, baptism for the dead, and temple endowment ceremonies. Smith was killed June 27, 1844, in Carthage, Illinois, by a mob that stormed the jail, making him the first U.S. presidential candidate to be assassinated. His death propelled the movement toward westward expansion under successor leadership.

joseph-smith-sr-1771.life_summary: Joseph Smith Sr. was born July 12, 1771, in Topsfield, Massachusetts, to Asael Smith and Mary Duty, with ancestry tracing to Robert Smith of Lincolnshire, England. In his early years, he was a Universalist, founding a Universalist society in Topsfield in 1797. He practiced folk religion including dream interpretation, divining rods, and treasure seeking, and struggled with depression managed through alcohol and visionary dreams. He married Lucy Mack on January 26, 1796, in Tunbridge, Vermont, and had eleven children together. Smith worked various occupations—farmer, teacher, and shopkeeper—with limited success. The death of his eldest son Alvin in 1823 disrupted his farming plans in Palmyra, New York. Despite financial struggles and personal hardship, he became a foundational figure in his son Joseph's religious movement.
joseph-smith-sr-1771.church_summary: Joseph Smith Sr. was baptized when the Church of Christ formally organized on April 6, 1830, becoming one of the church's first members. He was ordained the church's first Presiding Patriarch on December 18, 1833, and later served as Assistant Counselor in the First Presidency beginning September 3, 1837. He signed the Testimony of the Eight Witnesses in June 1829, attesting to the Book of Mormon plates. Smith relocated with his family to Far West, Missouri, in 1838 and later to Nauvoo, Illinois, in 1839, where he administered patriarchal blessings before his death. He died in Nauvoo on September 14, 1840, and was succeeded as Presiding Patriarch by his eldest surviving son, Hyrum.

l-tom-perry-1922.life_summary: Lowell Tom Perry was born August 5, 1922, in Logan, Utah, to a family with strong agricultural and business ties. He attended Utah State Agricultural College (now Utah State University), earning a bachelor's degree in finance in 1949. Perry worked in textile manufacturing and business management throughout much of his career, developing a reputation as a practical administrator with strong ethical standards. He was married twice: first to Virginia C. Lee in 1947, with whom he had multiple children, and after her death in 1974, he married Barbara Dayton in 1976. Perry maintained significant ties to his hometown of Logan throughout his life and was deeply involved in community and civic affairs.
l-tom-perry-1922.church_summary: Perry served as an LDS missionary in the Northern States Mission from 1942 to 1944, working in the Marion, Ohio, and Cedar Rapids, Iowa areas. He became an Assistant to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 1972 and was ordained as an apostle on April 11, 1974. Perry served as the Europe Central Area President from 2004 to 2015, based in Frankfurt, Germany, providing oversight for church operations across multiple European nations. His ministry focused on strengthening families and personal growth, and he was recognized for delivering compassionate talks emphasizing scripture study, service, and dedication to covenant principles.

legrand-richards-1886.life_summary: LeGrand Richards was born in Farmington, Utah Territory, in 1886 to George F. Richards and Alice Almira Robinson. He survived several dangerous childhood accidents, including being struck by an axe and having wagon wheels roll over his head, before reaching adulthood. He attended the 1893 Salt Lake Temple dedication as a youth. In 1909, he married Ina Jane Ashton, and they had eight children together. Richards combined his Church service with intellectual pursuits, authoring A Marvelous Work and a Wonder (1950), a comprehensive teaching outline widely used in missionary work, and Israel! Do You Know? (1955), which explored connections between Jewish and Mormon traditions. Spencer W. Kimball described him as one of the greatest missionaries of his time.
legrand-richards-1886.church_summary: Richards began his Church service with a proselytizing mission to the Netherlands from 1905 to 1908. He held various leadership positions including branch president in Portland (1909), presiding elder in the Netherlands (1914–1916), and bishop of a Salt Lake City ward (1920–1925). He served as president of the Hollywood Stake (1931–1933) and the Southern States Mission (1934–1937). From 1938 to 1952, Richards served as the seventh presiding bishop of the Church. He was then called to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and remained an active member until his death at age 96 in 1983. He was the longest-lived LDS apostle until David B. Haight, and both his father and grandfather served as President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles.

lorenzo-snow-1814.life_summary: Lorenzo Snow was born April 3, 1814, in Mantua, Ohio, in a well-educated Quaker family. His father was an artist and educator, providing Snow with intellectual formation and refinement unusual among his generation. He attended Oberlin College, one of the few higher education institutions open to young men of limited means, where he studied classical languages and philosophy. Snow became fluent in multiple languages and earned respect as a disciplined, philosophical thinker. Before his 1836 conversion to Mormonism, he had established himself as a schoolteacher and intellectual leader in his Ohio community, bringing both learning and social refinement to his faith.
lorenzo-snow-1814.church_summary: Snow served missions to England (1840–1843), Hawaii (1864), and the Holy Land (1871). Ordained an apostle in 1849, he became known for intellectual rigor and theological sophistication. As church president from 1898 to 1901, Snow articulated the doctrine of eternal progression through his famous couplet, framing the human potential to become divine. He served as Salt Lake Temple president (1893–1898), championing tithing as fundamental to religious membership. His ministry stressed financial commitment, education, and the elevation of Mormon theology through systematic doctrine. He led the church through financial recovery and institutional consolidation.

luke-johnson-1807.life_summary: Luke Johnson was born on November 3, 1807, in Pomfret, Vermont, during the early period of American independence and religious ferment. He grew up in Vermont during the wave of revivals and spiritual seeking that characterized the early 19th century. Johnson was an educated man who became an educator and physician, positioning himself to serve his community beyond purely ministerial roles. On November 1, 1833, he married Susan H. Poteet, and their union produced six children: Elisa Mary, Fanny, Eliza, Vashtia, James, and Solomon. When Susan died on September 20, 1846, Johnson eventually remarried on March 3, 1847, to America Morgan Clark in Council Bluffs, Iowa, with whom he fathered seven more children.
luke-johnson-1807.church_summary: Johnson was baptized early in the church's history and immediately engaged in missionary service. Beginning in 1831, he undertook missions to southern Ohio with Robert Rathburn and preached throughout Pennsylvania and Ohio with Sidney Rigdon. He was ordained to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles on February 15, 1835, serving until December 31, 1837. Following his departure from the apostleship, Johnson left the church for a period but was later rebaptized on March 8, 1846. After the church's migration to Utah, he participated in the Mormon Pioneer journey to Salt Lake Valley in July 1847 and subsequently served as Bishop of St. John in Tooele County, Utah. His life exemplified the 19th-century Latter-day Saint pattern of pioneering, family building, and service in various ecclesiastical and civic capacities.
luke-johnson-1807.death_place: Salt Lake City, Utah Territory, United States

lyman-e-johnson-1811.life_summary: Lyman Eugene Johnson was born on October 24, 1811, in Pomfret, Windsor County, Vermont, a region steeped in New England Calvinist tradition and frontier experience. He came of age during the Second Great Awakening and the rapid expansion of American settlement westward. On September 4, 1834, he married Sarah Susan Long, establishing a household that produced at least five children. Johnson was a man of ambition and capability, with talents for law, business, and civic organization that would define his later life. His journey from rural Vermont to the American frontier exemplified the restless energy and opportunity-seeking that characterized his generation.
lyman-e-johnson-1811.church_summary: Johnson began his missionary service in 1832, traveling with Orson Pratt throughout the eastern United States, and continued as a successful missionary from 1835 to 1837. He participated in Zion's Camp, the military expedition undertaken in summer 1834 to redeem lands in Missouri. He was called to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles on February 14, 1835, but his tenure was turbulent. He was removed from the Quorum of the Twelve on September 3, 1837, and subsequently excommunicated on April 13, 1838. After leaving the church, Johnson relocated to Iowa and Wisconsin, where he established himself as one of the founding figures of Keokuk, Iowa, and became a successful pioneer lawyer. He died on December 20, 1859, when his sleigh broke through an air-hole in the ice of the Mississippi River near Prairie du Chien, Wisconsin.
lyman-e-johnson-1811.birth_place: Pomfret, Windsor County, Vermont, United States
lyman-e-johnson-1811.death_place: Prairie du Chien, Wisconsin, United States

lyman-wight-1796.life_summary: Lyman Wight was born May 9, 1796, in Fairfield, New York, during the early years of American independence. He grew up in a rural area during a period of religious experimentation and frontier expansion. Wight was baptized into the Church of Christ by Oliver Cowdery on November 14, 1830, early in the movement's history. He married Harriet Benton on January 5, 1823, in Henrietta, New York, before his conversion and eventually married four wives in accordance with church polygamy doctrine, fathering eleven children. Wight was ordained to the high priesthood by Joseph Smith Jr. in June 1831, positioning him among the early ecclesiastical leaders of the rapidly growing movement.
lyman-wight-1796.church_summary: Wight served eleven missions as a member of the church and was ordained an apostle on April 8, 1841, to replace David W. Patten. Following Joseph Smith's death, Wight established separate communities in Texas, maintaining distinctive Latter-day Saint beliefs and practices. His followers built the first Latter-day Saint temple west of the Mississippi River in Zodiac, Texas, where members performed sealings, ordinations, washing and anointings, and adoption ceremonies. Wight's ministry emphasized community building and settlement establishment, and he was deeply involved in the tumultuous events of early church history in Missouri. His leadership demonstrated both the creativity and the sectarian divisions that characterized early Latter-day Saint expansion.

m-russell-ballard-1928.life_summary: Merrill Russell Ballard was born on October 8, 1928, in Salt Lake City, Utah. He grew up in a prominent LDS family with deep roots in church leadership and community service. Ballard received his education in Salt Lake City and developed a career as a prominent businessman and church administrator. He married Barbara Bowen on August 28, 1951, in the Salt Lake Temple, and the couple raised seven children together. Barbara preceded him in death on October 1, 2018, after more than six decades of marriage. Ballard established himself as a respected leader in both business and ecclesiastical circles, becoming a trusted figure in church administration and governance throughout his adult life.
m-russell-ballard-1928.church_summary: M. Russell Ballard served as a missionary in England from 1948 to 1950, serving as a counselor in the mission presidency. He was called to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles on October 6, 1985, and served in this capacity for 38 years until his death in 2023. Ballard served as President of the Canada Toronto Mission from 1974 to 1976 and held the position of Acting President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles from 2018 until his death. He also served as editor of church magazines from 1980 to 1984. As an apostle, he was sustained by church members as a prophet, seer, and revelator, and played a significant role in church administration and policy implementation.

marion-g-romney-1897.life_summary: Marion G. Romney was born September 19, 1897, in Colonia Juárez, Chihuahua, Mexico, to LDS pioneer settlers. His parents were among the Latter-day Saint colonists in Mexico, giving him an international and cross-cultural perspective unusual for his generation. Romney developed a deep commitment to agricultural development and community building, reflecting his pioneering heritage. He married Ida Jensen on September 12, 1924, in the Salt Lake Temple, and the couple had two biological sons, one of whom died in infancy, and one adopted child. Romney spent significant portions of his professional life focused on church welfare principles and Book of Mormon scholarship, emerging as a thought leader in both areas.
marion-g-romney-1897.church_summary: Romney served as a missionary in Australia from 1920 to 1923, gaining experience in international church work. He was called as an Assistant to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 1941 and became a member of the Quorum of the Twelve in 1951. From 1961 to 1972, he served as an area supervisor for Mexico, helping to strengthen the church's work in the land of his birth. He was appointed Second Counselor in the First Presidency in 1972, serving until 1982, when he became First Counselor until 1985. He concluded his service as Quorum President from 1985 until his death in 1988. Romney was renowned as a pioneer of church welfare initiatives and a careful student of Book of Mormon teachings.
marion-g-romney-1897.burial_place: Wasatch Lawn Memorial Park, Salt Lake City, Utah
teaching_emphasis: Book of Mormon scholarship and doctrine

mark-e-petersen-1900.life_summary: Mark Edward Petersen was born on November 7, 1900, in Salt Lake City, Utah. He grew up in a prominent LDS family and developed early interests in writing, journalism, and religious education. Petersen married Emma Marr McDonald in 1920, and together they built a life centered on religious scholarship and public communication. Before entering full-time Church service, Petersen worked as a journalist and editor, bringing his professional communication skills to bear on religious topics. His prolific literary output—over forty published books—reflected a lifetime of intellectual engagement with scripture, doctrine, and moral instruction. He passed away on January 11, 1984, leaving behind a substantial legacy of published works.
mark-e-petersen-1900.church_summary: Petersen served as a missionary in Nova Scotia during his youth. He was ordained to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 1944 and served in that capacity for four decades. Throughout his apostolic career, Petersen directed the Church's public information programs and authored extensively on topics including chastity, marriage, family life, and scriptural interpretation. He served as president of the West European Mission for six years and sat on numerous Church committees including those responsible for military relations, Indian affairs, and music. His prolific teaching ministry and extensive publications made him one of the twentieth century's most visible LDS theological voices.

marriner-w-merrill-1832.life_summary: Marriner Wood Merrill was born on September 25, 1832, in Sackville, New Brunswick, Canada. He joined the Latter-day Saint Church in April 1852 and immigrated to Salt Lake City in 1853, becoming one of the pioneering settlers of Cache Valley, Utah. Merrill developed a reputation as a dedicated administrator and community builder, establishing deep roots in the Richmond, Utah area. Over the course of his life, he raised an exceptionally large family, eventually having forty-six children. Beyond his ecclesiastical responsibilities, he served his community in numerous civic capacities, including as postmaster of Richmond and as a member of the territorial legislature, embodying the ideal of the pioneering saint.
marriner-w-merrill-1832.church_summary: Marriner W. Merrill served as bishop of Richmond for eighteen years beginning in July 1861. He was ordained to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles on October 7, 1889, and served as first president of Logan Temple beginning in 1884. He was also a counselor in the Cache Stake presidency from 1879 onward. Despite facing legal prosecution for unlawful cohabitation in 1889, from which he was quickly released, he remained active in Church leadership. He was summoned twice by Congress during the Smoot investigation but declined to appear. By his 1935 family reunion, his descendants numbered 797. He died on February 6, 1906, in Richmond, Utah.

marvin-j-ashton-1915.life_summary: Marvin Judson Ashton was born on May 6, 1915, in Salt Lake City, Utah, to a prominent local family. He grew up in the community and pursued education and early professional development during the Great Depression and World War II era. Ashton married Norma Berntson on August 22, 1940, in the Salt Lake Temple, and the couple had four children together. Beyond his church responsibilities, Ashton established himself as a respected family man and community member, maintaining strong ties to his native Utah throughout his life.
marvin-j-ashton-1915.church_summary: Ashton served as a missionary in Great Britain from 1937 to 1939, where he distinguished himself by editing the Millennial Star under mission president Hugh B. Brown. He ascended to prominence within the church hierarchy, being ordained as an apostle on December 2, 1971, a position he held until his death on February 25, 1994. During his apostolic tenure, Ashton focused on spiritual guidance and moral leadership, publishing works such as 'What Is Your Destination?' and 'Be of Good Cheer' that became widely read in church circles.

matthew-cowley-1897.life_summary: Matthew Cowley was born on August 2, 1897, in Preston, Idaho, in the northern part of the state. From an early age, he showed a calling toward missionary work and linguistic study. At age seventeen, he was called to serve in New Zealand, where he spent five years learning the Māori language and culture with remarkable proficiency. Cowley married Elva Eleanor Taylor on July 13, 1922, at the Salt Lake Temple, and they had one daughter, Jewell. After his initial mission, he pursued professional responsibilities while maintaining Church leadership. His life was marked by compassion, eloquence, and a distinctive ability to communicate across cultural boundaries, talents he would employ throughout his ecclesiastical career.
matthew-cowley-1897.church_summary: Cowley served as a missionary in New Zealand from 1914 to 1919, where he translated the Book of Mormon into Māori (published 1917) and the Doctrine and Covenants and Pearl of Great Price (published 1919). He later served as New Zealand Mission President from 1938 to 1945, providing leadership during critical war years. He was ordained as an apostle on October 11, 1945, and in 1946 was assigned president of the Pacific Missions, overseeing Hawaiian, Samoan, Tongan, Australian, and other regional missions. Cowley became known for his emphasis on compassion and his call to openly welcome sinners rather than ostracize them. His sermons were compiled posthumously in Matthew Cowley Speaks (1954).

matthias-f-cowley-1858.life_summary: Matthias Foss Cowley was born on August 25, 1858, in Salt Lake City, Utah Territory, and spent his formative years in the heart of the Mormon community. He came of age during the Church's most challenging period, as federal prosecution of polygamy intensified. Cowley became known as a devoted family man and prolific writer on Church doctrine and history. His marriage to Abbie Hyde produced LDS apostle Matthew Cowley, who became a prominent twentieth-century Church leader. His second marriage to Luella Parkinson produced Samuel P. Cowley, who served as an FBI agent before being killed in 1934. Cowley maintained an active intellectual life, publishing five major works on Church doctrine and history between 1902 and 1963.
matthias-f-cowley-1858.church_summary: Matthias F. Cowley was ordained an apostle on October 7, 1897, by Wilford Woodruff, replacing Moses Thatcher in the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles. He served in this position until October 28, 1905, when he resigned at the request of Joseph F. Smith, partly due to his involvement in performing marriages that contravened the Church's 1890 Manifesto against plural marriage. His priesthood was suspended on May 11, 1911, but was restored on April 3, 1936. However, he was never restored to his former position in the Quorum. The town of Cowley, Wyoming was named in his honor. He died on June 16, 1940, in Salt Lake City, from uremia resulting from kidney failure.
matthias-f-cowley-1858.birth_place: Salt Lake City, Utah Territory, United States
matthias-f-cowley-1858.death_place: Salt Lake City, Utah, United States
