melvin-j-ballard-1873.life_summary: Melvin J. Ballard was born on February 9, 1873, in Logan, Utah Territory. He was raised in the early Utah community during the pioneering era of the LDS Church. Ballard received his education in Utah schools and developed into a respected church leader and administrator. He married Martha A. Jones in June 1896, and the couple built a life together centered on church service. Ballard became known for his dedication to expanding church influence and missionary work, particularly through innovative approaches to reaching new populations. His legacy extended beyond his lifetime through his descendants, most notably his grandson M. Russell Ballard, who also became a prominent apostle in the twentieth century.
melvin-j-ballard-1873.church_summary: Melvin J. Ballard served in the Eastern United States and Northern States missions from 1896 to 1898, then presided over the Northwestern States Mission where he pioneered Native American missionary work in Montana. He was instrumental in opening South American missionary work, establishing the church's presence in Buenos Aires, Argentina, in 1925. Ballard was ordained an apostle and became a member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles on January 7, 1919. He served in this capacity until his death in 1939 from leukemia. His ministry emphasized revelation and divine inspiration to church leadership, with particular focus on righteousness and spiritual conviction among church members.

mission.location: Eastern United States and Northern States

moses-thatcher-1842.life_summary: Moses Thatcher was born on February 2, 1842, in Sangamon County, Illinois, during the early period of Latter-day Saint settlement in the Midwest. He grew up within the Church community and received his basic education before the Thatcher family relocated to Utah Territory as part of the great exodus of Mormon pioneers. As a young man, Thatcher became known for his dedication to community service and his willingness to take on responsibility. He developed a reputation as a thoughtful and principled leader, qualities that would define his long tenure in Church leadership. Throughout his life, he remained engaged in both ecclesiastical and civic affairs in Utah Territory.
moses-thatcher-1842.church_summary: Moses Thatcher served as a missionary beginning at age 15, completing his first mission in 1858, and later served in the United Kingdom and France (1866-1868) and as a mission president in Mexico (1879-1880). He was ordained as an apostle in April 1879 and served in the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles until 1896, when he was removed over disagreement regarding church control of public office-seeking. He remained in good standing and retained his apostolic priesthood office until his death in 1909 at age 67. He also served as second assistant to Wilford Woodruff in the Young Men's Mutual Improvement Association from 1880 to 1898.

nathan-eldon-tanner-1898.life_summary: Nathan Eldon Tanner was born May 11, 1898, in Salt Lake City, Utah, into an influential Latter-day Saint family. He developed a distinguished career in business and finance, becoming known for his sharp administrative mind and ethical principles. Tanner earned advanced education and worked as an accountant and business executive, holding leadership positions in various corporate and civic organizations. He married Sara Isabelle Johnson in 1920, and together they built a family centered on church principles and community service. Tanner's background in finance and business administration made him invaluable to church leadership seeking professional management of institutional resources.
nathan-eldon-tanner-1898.church_summary: Tanner served as an Assistant to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles starting in 1942 and was ordained as a member of the Quorum of the Twelve in 1956. He became Second Counselor in the First Presidency in 1960 and served in that position for nearly twenty years, managing the church's temporal affairs with noted efficiency. Tanner was known for his emphasis on financial honesty, prudent resource management, and the principle of paying tithes and offerings to support the church's mission. He helped establish the church's international growth initiatives and served as a trusted advisor to multiple church presidents. His ministry focused on helping members understand the practical application of gospel principles in their daily financial and family lives.

neal-a-maxwell-1926.life_summary: Neal Ash Maxwell was born on July 6, 1926, in Salt Lake City, Utah, into a family deeply rooted in the Latter-day Saint community. He served his country during World War II before undertaking a two-year mission to Canada. Maxwell married Colleen Hinckley on November 22, 1950; she was the daughter of church leader Gordon B. Hinckley. Together they had four children and twenty-four grandchildren. Maxwell's intellectual prowess and eloquent speaking style set him apart from his peers, earning him recognition as one of the most gifted communicators in the twentieth-century church. He authored approximately thirty books on gospel-related subjects, establishing himself as a prolific religious scholar.
neal-a-maxwell-1926.church_summary: Maxwell served as an LDS Church missionary in Canada for two years following his World War II military service. He became renowned for his eloquent and highly alliterative approach to religious instruction, employing such linguistic complexity that church conference translators ranked his presentations at the highest difficulty level. His works focused on religious scholarship and brought vivid imagery to gospel teachings. Church President Gordon B. Hinckley remarked that each of Maxwell's talks was a masterpiece and each book a work of art. Despite being diagnosed with leukemia in 1996, Maxwell continued his apostolic duties until his death on July 21, 2004, leaving behind a legacy of literary and spiritual eloquence.

neil-l-andersen-1951.life_summary: Neil Loren Andersen was born on August 9, 1951, in Logan, Utah. He grew up in northern Utah during the post-war era and pursued an education that prepared him for both business and ecclesiastical leadership. Before his full-time service in the Church leadership, Andersen developed a successful career while maintaining active involvement in his local congregation. He married Kathy Sue Williams on March 20, 1975, at the Salt Lake Temple, and together they raised their family while he progressed through various Church assignments. His early life balanced professional ambitions with religious commitment, eventually leading him to prioritize full-time Church service and administration.
neil-l-andersen-1951.church_summary: Andersen served as a missionary in France during his youth and later served as president of the Church's France Bordeaux Mission from 1989 to 1992, demonstrating a deep connection to French culture and language. He was called to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 2014. His ministry has emphasized marriage and family values, including opposition to practices that undermine traditional family structures. He has presided over temple groundbreakings, including the Twin Falls Idaho Temple (2006) and the Gila Valley Arizona Temple (2009). His teaching focuses on the importance of strong marriages and families as foundations of society and personal spiritual development.

oliver-cowdery-1806.life_summary: Oliver Hypram Cowdery was born on October 3, 1806, in Wells, Vermont, during the early years of American independence. He grew up in the rural northeastern United States and received education befitting his era and social station. Cowdery married Elizabeth Ann Whitmer on December 18, 1832, in a union that produced six children, though only one daughter survived to adulthood—a tragically common pattern in nineteenth-century frontier America. Despite his central role in the founding of the Latter Day Saint movement, Cowdery's later life was marked by apostasy and exile, before he sought reconciliation with the church in his final years.
oliver-cowdery-1806.church_summary: Oliver Cowdery served as the principal scribe for the Book of Mormon and was the first person baptized into the restored church, serving as one of the Three Witnesses to the golden plates. He was ordained as a founding apostle and held membership in the First Presidency in Kirtland. Cowdery played key roles as a missionary during the formative period of the movement in the 1820s and 1830s, helping to establish foundational practices and doctrine. However, he became estranged from the church due to conflicts with Joseph Smith and others, leading to excommunication. He died on March 3, 1850, at David Whitmer's home in Richmond, Missouri, having sought renewed fellowship with the church before his death.

orson-f-whitney-1855.life_summary: Orson Fisher Whitney was born July 1, 1855, in Salt Lake City, the son of Orson Spencer and Catherine Curtis. He grew up in the heart of the LDS community and inherited a tradition of intellectual and literary achievement from his father, a prominent theologian and educator. Whitney developed early talents in poetry and historical narrative while contributing to Church periodicals and teaching at educational institutions. His civic service in Salt Lake City as city treasurer (1884–1890) and state senator (1898, 1901) demonstrated his integration into Utah's emerging political establishment. He balanced secular responsibilities with ecclesiastical duties, establishing himself as an intellectual voice in Mormon intellectual circles.
orson-f-whitney-1855.church_summary: Whitney served missions to Pennsylvania, Ohio, and Europe (1881–1883), where he edited the Millennial Star, a major Church publication. He taught English and theology at Brigham Young College and served as Assistant Church Historian before his ordination as an apostle on April 8, 1906. As a poet and publicist, he became known for composing hymn texts and authoring historical and biographical works that articulated Mormon identity. He maintained the position of apostle until his death in 1931, serving over 25 years in the Quorum of the Twelve and contributing to the Church's scholarly and artistic dimension.
teaching_emphasis: Poetry and artistic expression of faith
Journalism as a vehicle for doctrine

orson-hyde-1805.life_summary: Orson Hyde was born on January 8, 1805, in Oxford, Connecticut, where he spent his childhood in the religious ferment of New England. He came of age during the Second Great Awakening, a period of intense spiritual seeking and revival that characterized early 19th-century America. In 1834, he married Marinda Nancy Johnson in Kirtland, Ohio, beginning a family that would eventually encompass eight wives and thirty-two children, as he embraced the practice of plural marriage that would become central to later Latter-day Saint doctrine. Hyde developed a reputation as a devoted and courageous missionary, willing to travel to distant lands in service of his faith.
orson-hyde-1805.church_summary: Hyde was ordained an apostle on February 15, 1835, and became a prominent figure in church leadership, serving as president of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles from December 27, 1847, until June 1875. He undertook remarkable missionary journeys: in 1831–1832 he proselytized throughout the eastern United States; in 1837–1838 he led a mission to Great Britain that resulted in approximately 1,500 converts; and most famously, from 1840–1842 he traveled to Jerusalem, where he performed a dedicatory prayer on the Mount of Olives on October 24, 1841. He served as president of a British mission from 1846–1847 and led important settlement expeditions to Carson Valley, Nevada, and the Sanpete-Sevier District. As an associate judge for Utah Territory from 1852 onwards, he wielded civic authority. Hyde oversaw completion of the Nauvoo Temple, which was dedicated in 1846. An Orson Hyde Memorial Garden was dedicated to his memory in Jerusalem in 1979.
orson-hyde-1805.death_place: Spring City, Utah Territory, United States

mission.location: Eastern United States, Great Britain, and Jerusalem

orson-pratt-1811.life_summary: Orson Pratt Sr. was born in Hartford, New York, and became one of the Church's most intellectually prominent leaders. A gifted mathematician and astronomer, he authored sixteen theological pamphlets and two mathematics books, earning renown as a scholar within the LDS movement. Pratt was educated in the rapidly developing American frontier context and channeled his analytical mind toward theological argumentation. He fathered approximately forty-five children across multiple marriages and remained a prolific writer throughout his life, defending polygamy as a central tenet of Latter-day Saint doctrine.
orson-pratt-1811.church_summary: Pratt was baptized in 1830 and ordained an Elder that same year, serving numerous short-term missions across the northeastern United States. In 1835, Joseph Smith called him to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles. He served a British mission from 1839 to 1841 and faced a major crisis when excommunicated on August 20, 1842, following accusations involving Smith and his wife, though he was reinstated in January 1843. Under Brigham Young's leadership, Pratt was frequently sent on missions to minimize his ecclesiastical influence. He served as Church Historian and Speaker of the Utah House, earning the title "apostle of polygamy" for his vocal theological defense of that practice.

parley-p-pratt-1807.life_summary: Parley Parker Pratt was born on April 12, 1807, in Burlington, New York. He grew up in rural New York during the early nineteenth century and received modest education before his conversion to the LDS faith. Pratt worked as a laborer and tradesman before dedicating himself fully to religious work. He became one of the most prolific writers and missionaries in early LDS history, authoring 31 published works including the theological treatise 'A Voice of Warning,' published in 1837, which became influential in LDS missionary work. Pratt married his first wife, Thankful Halsey, on September 9, 1827, and subsequently married Mary Ann Frost Stearns on May 14, 1837, and ultimately married a total of twelve women throughout his lifetime. He traveled extensively throughout North America and internationally, establishing himself as a prominent voice for LDS theology and doctrine.
parley-p-pratt-1807.church_summary: Parley P. Pratt was one of the original members of the Quorum of Twelve Apostles, called in 1835. He served numerous missions throughout his apostolic career, including work in New York, New England, and eastern Canada in 1835; Upper Canada and Toronto in 1836; New York City from 1837 to 1838; the Southern United States, England, and Pacific islands; and Chile in Valparaíso where he conducted missionary work until 1852. He served as presiding officer of the Pacific Mission in 1854 and undertook missionary work in Great Britain from 1839 to 1841. Pratt returned to the Eastern United States in 1856. He also served as editor of the Millennial Star, an important LDS publication, from 1839. Pratt's scholarly theological writings helped establish doctrinal foundations for the growing church.

patrick-kearon-1961.life_summary: Patrick Richard Kearon was born on July 18, 1961, in Carlisle, England. He grew up in post-war England and pursued education and professional development that prepared him for humanitarian and ecclesiastical leadership. Before his full-time Church service, Kearon worked in humanitarian and social justice contexts, developing expertise in refugee assistance, human rights protection, and supporting survivors of violence and oppression. He married Jennifer Carole Hulme in 1991 at the Oakland California Temple after meeting her, a BYU student, in London. The couple has four children, though their eldest child passed away at three weeks old from a heart condition—an experience that deepened their compassion for suffering families. His professional background in humanitarian work informed his subsequent Church leadership.
patrick-kearon-1961.church_summary: Kearon began full-time service in the Church as a general authority in 2010, bringing his humanitarian expertise to Church assignments. He was called to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 2018. His ministry has emphasized religious freedom and protecting the rights of all people regardless of faith background, spiritual healing through Jesus Christ's atonement, humanitarian service particularly regarding refugee assistance, and supporting survivors of abuse, violence, and oppression. His personal experience with grief and his professional background in humanitarian work have enabled him to address the needs of vulnerable and marginalized populations with particular compassion and understanding, making him a voice for the suffering and dispossessed.
teaching_emphasis: Compassion for the suffering and vulnerable

quentinl-cook-1940.life_summary: Quentin Larson Cook was born on September 8, 1940, in Logan, Utah. He grew up in northern Utah and received his education in Logan schools before attending Brigham Young University. Cook married Mary Gaddie on November 30, 1962, in the Logan Utah Temple, and the couple raised three children together. Cook developed a career in law and business before his increasing involvement in church leadership roles. He became known for his intellectual rigor, legal expertise, and thoughtful approach to complex ecclesiastical and administrative matters. Cook maintained his professional credentials while simultaneously advancing through church positions, demonstrating his ability to balance secular and religious responsibilities.
quentinl-cook-1940.church_summary: Quentin L. Cook served as an LDS Church missionary in England from 1960 to 1962, where he served alongside Jeffrey R. Holland as companions, with Marion D. Hanks serving as mission president. He was called to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles on October 6, 2007, and holds the fifth most senior apostle position in church leadership. As an apostle, Cook is sustained by church members as a prophet, seer, and revelator. His published works demonstrate his emphasis on interfaith collaboration and cooperation with individuals of other faiths, as evidenced by his publication of 'Partnering with Our Friends from Other Faiths' in 2010. Cook has focused on building bridges between the LDS Church and other religious traditions.
teaching_emphasis: Legal and intellectual rigor in spiritual matters

reed-smoot-1862.life_summary: Reed Smoot was born on January 10, 1862, in Salt Lake City, Utah Territory. He attended Brigham Young Academy (the precursor to Brigham Young University) and served a missionary mission in England after graduating in 1879. Upon his return, Smoot established himself as a man of keen intellect and political acumen. He brought to his public service a unique combination of deep religious conviction and sophisticated understanding of national politics and economics. His marriage to Alpha M. Eldredge on September 17, 1884, produced six children. Throughout his life, Smoot demonstrated exceptional skill in navigating the complex intersection of religious belief and secular governance during a transformative period in American history.
reed-smoot-1862.church_summary: Reed Smoot was ordained as an apostle and member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles on April 8, 1900. Simultaneously, he pursued a prominent political career, being elected as a Republican U.S. Senator from Utah in 1902 and serving from 1903 to 1933. He faced intense scrutiny during the four-year Reed Smoot Hearings (1904-1907) before the Senate Committee on Privileges and Elections regarding his eligibility to serve based on his Church membership. As chairman of the Senate Finance Committee from 1923 to 1933, he co-sponsored the 1930 Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act. He also supported National Park Service legislation in 1916. At his death on February 9, 1941, in St. Petersburg, Florida, he held the third position in the Church succession line, a testament to his esteem within the organization.
reed-smoot-1862.birth_place: Salt Lake City, Utah Territory, United States

richard-g-scott-1928.life_summary: Richard Garn Scott was born November 7, 1928, in Pocatello, Idaho. He grew up in a devoted Latter-day Saint family with connections to the Pacific Northwest. Scott pursued engineering and technical education, which became foundational to his professional career in various technical and administrative roles. He married Jeanene Watkins on July 16, 1953, in the Manti Temple, and they built a strong partnership centered on church service and family. Jeanene passed away in 1995 after battling cancer, a loss that deepened Scott's compassion and spiritual insight. Throughout his secular career, Scott maintained a balance between professional responsibility and church service, developing a reputation for both competence and spiritual integrity.
richard-g-scott-1928.church_summary: Scott served as a missionary in the Uruguay Montevideo Mission from 1950 to 1953 and later became the Argentina North Mission President from 1965 to 1968. He became a general authority and member of the First Quorum of the Seventy in 1977, advancing to the Presidency of the Seventy in 1983. He was ordained to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 1988 and served in that capacity until his death in 2015. Throughout his ministry, Scott was known for delivering compassionate talks that emphasized repentance, Jesus Christ's forgiveness, the healing power of the atonement, and the importance of truth in personal decision-making. His teachings frequently addressed helping those who had experienced abuse or trauma.

richard-l-evans-1906.life_summary: Richard Louis Evans was born in 1906 in Salt Lake City, Utah. He grew up in the early twentieth-century LDS community and developed a distinctive gift for public communication and broadcasting. Evans received his education in Salt Lake Valley schools and pursued studies in music and communications. He became a prominent voice in religious broadcasting during the golden age of radio, developing a distinctive style of spiritual commentary that appealed to both Church members and the broader American public. Evans married and established a family while building his career in communications. His talent for translating religious concepts into language accessible to mainstream audiences made him a unique figure in twentieth-century LDS leadership.
richard-l-evans-1906.church_summary: Evans served as a missionary in European missions during his youth. He became best known for his role as the host and narrator of the Tabernacle Choir at Temple Square radio program, one of the longest-running radio programs in American broadcasting history. He was ordained as a member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and served in that capacity for many years, bringing his communication expertise to apostolic ministry. Evans was deeply involved in transmitting LDS messages through the modern media of radio and television, helping the Church reach millions of Americans during the twentieth century. His distinctive voice and thoughtful presentation of doctrine made him one of the most recognizable LDS leaders of his era.

richard-r-lyman-1870.life_summary: Richard Roswell Lyman was born in 1870 and came from a prominent LDS family—his father was Francis M. Lyman and his grandfather was Amasa M. Lyman, both apostles. Lyman pursued higher education in engineering, earning a master's degree from the University of Chicago in 1903 and a PhD from Cornell University in 1905. His professional career centered on civil engineering, with significant contributions to road construction and water measurement systems. He received the prestigious J. James R. Croes Gold Medal in 1915 for his engineering work and served as vice-chairman of the Utah State Road Commission and city engineer of Provo. He married Amy Brown in 1896 after eight years of courtship; she later became the eighth Relief Society general president.
richard-r-lyman-1870.church_summary: Lyman was appointed to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 1918 and served until 1943. His wife Amy Brown Lyman served as Relief Society general president from 1940 to 1945. In 1943, Church leaders discovered Lyman's long-standing intimate relationship with another woman, and he was excommunicated on November 12, 1943, for violating the law of chastity. At age 83, he was rebaptized on October 27, 1954, though not reinstated as an apostle. When he died on December 31, 1963, his full priesthood blessings were later restored posthumously in 1970.
richard-r-lyman-1870.death_place: Salt Lake City, Utah, United States

rm-nelson-1924.life_summary: Russell Marion Nelson Sr. was born on September 9, 1924, and became one of the twentieth century's most accomplished cardiac surgeons before his religious leadership. He participated in the first human open-heart surgery using cardiopulmonary bypass in 1951 and performed the first open-heart surgery in the United States west of the Mississippi River. Over his surgical career, he completed nearly 7,000 operations and served as president of the Society for Vascular Surgery. Nelson married twice: first to Dantzel White in 1945, with whom he had ten children until her death in 2005, and then to Wendy L. Watson in 2006. He was renowned in both medical and religious circles for his dedication to rigorous scholarship and innovation.
rm-nelson-1924.church_summary: Nelson served in various LDS Church positions before his 1984 appointment to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles. He became quorum president in 2015 and was called as president of the Church in 2018, serving in that capacity until his death on September 27, 2025, at age 101. His presidency emphasized international expansion and temple construction, with the announcement of 200 new temples worldwide. He implemented significant organizational changes, including the 2019 reversal of a controversial 2015 policy regarding same-sex couples. Nelson visited dozens of countries throughout his tenure, addressing thousands of Church members and establishing the Church's global presence as a central focus of his administration.
rm-nelson-1924.death_place: Salt Lake City, Utah, United States

robert-d-hales-1932.life_summary: Robert Dean Hales was born August 24, 1932, in New York City to a family with business and civic connections. He earned his bachelor's degree in business administration and developed a successful career in accounting and business administration. Hales served in the United States Air Force, where he gained additional leadership experience and discipline that shaped his approach to church service. He married Mary Crandall on June 10, 1953, in the Salt Lake Temple, and together they raised two sons. The Hales family maintained strong community ties throughout their lives, and Robert became known for his emphasis on the practical application of church welfare principles and his integrity in financial stewardship.
robert-d-hales-1932.church_summary: Hales was called as a general authority in 1975 as an Assistant to the Quorum of the Twelve, serving in the First Quorum of the Seventy from 1976 to 1985. He was then appointed Presiding Bishop of the Church from 1985 to 1994, overseeing the church's extensive welfare program and administrative operations. He was ordained as an apostle on April 7, 1994, and served in the Quorum of the Twelve until his death in 2017. Hales was heavily involved in church expansion in Europe, including work on the development of the East Germany Temple and the Manhattan New York Temple. His ministry consistently emphasized the importance of the church's welfare program and helping members achieve self-reliance.

ronald-a-rasband-1951.life_summary: Ronald Anderson Rasband was born on February 6, 1951, in Salt Lake City, Utah. He grew up in Utah's capital and pursued a business career that spanned multiple sectors and industries. Before dedicating himself to full-time Church service, Rasband established himself as a successful entrepreneur and business leader, bringing practical experience in commerce and organizational management. In 1973, he married Melanie Twitchell, and together they raised five children while managing a busy professional life. His business background provided him with administrative expertise and an understanding of organizational dynamics that would later inform his Church leadership responsibilities.
ronald-a-rasband-1951.church_summary: Rasband served as a missionary in the Eastern States Mission, covering the New York Metro area, western New York, and Pennsylvania during his early adult years. He was called to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 2015 and served as an Area President responsible for the Europe Central Area. During his area assignment, he oversaw the construction of the first chapel the Church built in the Czech Republic, demonstrating his commitment to expanding the Church's physical presence in formerly restricted regions. His ministry has focused on administrative excellence and the practical implementation of Church programs and initiatives across diverse geographic and cultural contexts.
ronald-a-rasband-1951.birth_place: Salt Lake City, Utah, United States

mission.location: Eastern States Mission (New York Metro, Western New York, Pennsylvania)

rudger-clawson-1857.life_summary: Rudger Judd Clawson was born on March 12, 1857, in Salt Lake City, Utah Territory, the son of Hiram Bradley Clawson and Margaret Judd. He grew up in the heart of the Salt Lake Valley during the formative years of the Utah Territory. As a young man, Clawson developed a deep commitment to missionary work and ecclesiastical service. His missionary experience profoundly shaped his character: in July 1879, while serving in Georgia, his companion Joseph Standing was killed by a mob at Varnell Station, yet Clawson faced the armed mob with composure and conviction, refusing to be intimidated. This early experience of persecution and faithfulness established him as a model of moral courage and steadfast devotion.
rudger-clawson-1857.church_summary: Rudger Clawson served as a missionary in Georgia and was ordained an apostle on October 10, 1898. He served continuously in the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles for forty-five years until his death in 1943. From 1921 to 1943, he served as President of the Quorum, holding this position for twenty-two years, the second-longest tenure in that office. In 1901, he was briefly called as Second Counselor in the First Presidency under Lorenzo Snow, serving for five days. He was the first polygamist convicted under the Edmunds Act in August 1882, receiving a sentence of three and a half years plus a $1,500 fine. He was pardoned by President Grover Cleveland in 1887. In 1904, the town of Kingsville, Utah, was renamed Clawson in his honor. He died on June 21, 1943, in Salt Lake City, from pneumonia at age 86.
rudger-clawson-1857.birth_place: Salt Lake City, Utah Territory, United States
rudger-clawson-1857.death_place: Salt Lake City, Utah, United States
rudger-clawson-1857.burial_place: Salt Lake City Cemetery, Salt Lake City, Utah

spencerw-kimball-1895.life_summary: Spencer Woolley Kimball was born on March 28, 1895, in Salt Lake City, Utah Territory, into the prominent Kimball family with deep roots in LDS Church history and leadership. He grew up in Salt Lake City and received his education in Utah schools during the early twentieth century. Kimball married Camilla Eyring on November 16, 1917, in a civil ceremony, and the couple was sealed in the temple on June 7, 1918. They raised four children together: Spencer L., Olive Beth, Andrew E., and Edward L. Camilla was born in 1894 and outlived her husband by two years, passing away in 1987. Kimball developed a career in church service while maintaining his commitment to family life, becoming widely respected for his compassion, integrity, and spiritual sensitivity throughout the Utah community.
spencerw-kimball-1895.church_summary: Spencer W. Kimball was called to serve in the Swiss-German Mission in June 1914, but due to World War I circumstances, was reassigned to the Central States Mission in Missouri, where he served until 1916. He advanced through the ranks of church leadership, eventually being called to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and ultimately serving as President of the LDS Church. As president, Kimball announced the construction of 27 temples and personally dedicated four of them. He served until his death in 1985, living to the age of 90 and passing away in November after a lengthy funeral service held on November 9, 1985. His ministry emphasized missionary service for able-bodied young men, repentance and forgiveness, sexual morality standards, Native American welfare and education, and spoke against racism and prejudice within church membership.

stephen-l-richards-1879.life_summary: Stephen Lyman Richards was born June 18, 1879, in Mendon, Utah Territory, to a family with deep roots in early Mormonism. The grandson of Willard Richards, a prominent apostle and pioneer, Stephen inherited a legacy of ecclesiastical leadership and intellectual achievement. He pursued rigorous legal training at the University of Utah and Columbia University Law School, earning his J.D. in 1904. Richards established a successful law practice in Salt Lake City and taught law at his alma mater, building a reputation as a skilled advocate and jurist. His combination of legal expertise and religious commitment made him an ideal bridge between the Church's temporal and spiritual operations.
stephen-l-richards-1879.church_summary: Richards was called as an apostle in 1917 at age 37 and served in the Quorum of the Twelve for over 40 years. He oversaw the Church's radio, publicity, and missionary literature efforts, modernizing Church communications during the mid-twentieth century. As First Counselor to President David O. McKay (1951–1959), he was instrumental in the post-war expansion of the Church and mentored younger leaders, including Gordon B. Hinckley. His teachings emphasized character development, legal and civic responsibility, and the relationship between Mormonism and American democracy. He demonstrated that ecclesiastical authority and secular expertise could be harmonized in service to the Church's mission.

sylvester-q-cannon-1877.life_summary: Sylvester Quayle Cannon was born on June 10, 1877, in Salt Lake City, Utah Territory, as the son of apostle George Q. Cannon. He received advanced technical education, earning a degree in mining engineering from MIT and studying at the University of Utah. Cannon pursued a professional career in mining and engineering, applying his technical expertise to Church business interests and community development in Utah. His intellectual rigor and administrative acumen made him a natural fit for leadership roles. He married and established a family while maintaining his professional responsibilities in the growing Utah economy.
sylvester-q-cannon-1877.church_summary: Cannon began his missionary service in Belgium in 1899 and became president of the Netherlands–Belgium Mission from 1900 to 1902. He also accompanied apostle Francis M. Lyman on a significant three-month journey through the Mediterranean and Middle East. Cannon served as Presiding Bishop of the LDS Church from 1925 to 1938, providing administrative oversight of Church welfare and temporal affairs. He was ordained as an apostle in 1938, initially holding the unique status of an associate member of the Quorum of the Twelve before becoming a full member in 1939. He served in the Quorum until his death in 1943.

thomas-b-marsh-1800.life_summary: Thomas Billings Marsh was born on November 1, 1800, in Acton, Massachusetts, during the early years of American independence. He grew up in New England during a period of significant religious ferment and social change. In 1820, he married Elizabeth Godkin in New York City, establishing his family roots in the northeastern United States. Marsh lived through the formative decades of the 19th century, witnessing America's westward expansion and the religious revivals that swept across the nation. He was drawn to spiritual seeking and became interested in new religious movements that promised restoration of ancient Christian practices and divine authority.
thomas-b-marsh-1800.church_summary: Marsh was baptized on September 3, 1830, by David Whitmer and quickly rose in church leadership. He was ordained a high priest in spring 1831 and called to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles on February 14–15, 1835, becoming its president on April 25, 1835. He received Doctrine and Covenants section 31, which described him as a 'physician to the church.' However, following disagreements with church leadership in 1838, Marsh left the church on October 19, 1838, and was excommunicated on March 17, 1839. He was eventually rebaptized on July 16, 1857, in Florence, Nebraska, and spent his final years in Ogden, Utah Territory.

thomas-s-monson-1927.life_summary: Thomas Spencer Monson was born August 21, 1927, at St. Mark's Hospital in Salt Lake City, Utah, to a respected family in the church community. He attended the University of Utah, where he majored in business administration, developing skills in leadership, organization, and practical management. Monson worked as a manager for the Deseret News Publishing Company, where he gained experience in media, publishing, and organizational administration. Throughout his secular career, Monson was known for his character, attention to detail, and genuine concern for individual people. His professional background in publishing and business management provided practical experience in communication and institutional leadership that served him well in ecclesiastical roles. He maintained strong connections to his Salt Lake City community and family throughout his life.
thomas-s-monson-1927.church_summary: Monson served as mission president to the Canadian Mission (Ontario and Quebec) from April 1959 to January 1962, overseeing 130–180 missionaries. Ordained an apostle in 1963, he advanced through leadership positions and became counselor to church presidents before his election as president in 2008, following Gordon B. Hinckley's death. As church president from 2008 to 2014, Monson led the denomination through major transitions and established fourteen new temple dedications and four rededications, including Rexburg Idaho, Draper Utah, Oquirrh Mountain Utah, Gilbert Arizona, and Phoenix Arizona temples. His ministry emphasized faith, service, spiritual development, and compassionate action. Monson was known for personal warmth and genuine care for individual members.

ulisses-soares-1958.life_summary: Ulisses Soares was born on October 2, 1958, in São Paulo, Brazil. He grew up in South America during a period of significant social and economic change and pursued education that prepared him for business and Church leadership roles. Before his full-time Church appointment, Soares established a successful business career in Brazil while maintaining deep involvement in his local congregation. In October 1982, he married Rosana Fernandes Morgado at the São Paulo Brazil Temple, and together they raised three children. His background as a Brazilian business leader brought practical experience in organizational management and cross-cultural communication to his subsequent Church responsibilities.
ulisses-soares-1958.church_summary: Soares served as a missionary in the Brazil Rio de Janeiro Mission beginning in early 1978, where he developed deep roots in Brazilian culture and the Church's presence in South America. He later served as president of the Portugal Porto Mission from 2000 to 2003, extending his international leadership experience to Europe. He was called to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 2005. His ministry has centered on the principle that the gospel is about people rather than programs, emphasizing relational and human-centered ministry. He dedicated the Fortaleza Brazil Temple in June 2019 and the Arequipa Peru Temple in December 2019, and participated in multiple other temple dedications across the Americas and Europe.

mission.location: Brazil Rio de Janeiro; Portugal Porto (mission president 2000–2003)

wilford-woodruff-1807.life_summary: Wilford Woodruff was born March 1, 1807, in Connecticut to a farming family. He received limited formal education but developed skills as a mechanic and craftsman before his religious awakening. Converted to the LDS faith in 1836, Woodruff brought a methodical mind and entrepreneurial spirit to the emerging church. His secular accomplishments included developing farmland, establishing mills, and serving in civic capacities in Utah Territory during the early territorial years. He became known for meticulous record-keeping and documentation, traits that defined both his personal business practices and his later ecclesiastical roles.
wilford-woodruff-1807.church_summary: Woodruff served missions to the United States, England (1839–1841), and eastern states, baptizing hundreds of converts. He was ordained an apostle in 1839 and participated in the exodus to Utah. As president of the Salt Lake Temple from 1877, he championed temple ordinances, genealogy, and ancestral sealing work. In 1887, he became church president, leading the denomination through the discontinuation of plural marriage in 1890. He dedicated or oversee completion of the St. George, Manti, and Salt Lake temples. His ministry emphasized genealogical research, temple theology, and economic self-sufficiency.

william-e-mclellin-1806.life_summary: William Earl McLellin was born on January 18, 1806, in Smith County, Tennessee, growing up in the frontier society of the American South. He developed intellectual interests in education and writing, becoming a teacher of penmanship. In 1829, he married Cynthia Ann, though she died two years later in 1831. He then married Emeline Miller in 1832 in Portage County, Ohio, and with her fathered six children: four sons and two daughters. His life spanned most of the 19th century, a period marked by American territorial expansion, political turbulence, and the development of new religious movements.
william-e-mclellin-1806.church_summary: McLellin was baptized on August 20, 1831, by Hyrum Smith in Paris, Illinois, and was ordained as an elder in the Church of Christ. He served multiple missions throughout the eastern United States, Missouri, and Illinois, including a mission with Joseph Smith himself to Tennessee. Called to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles on February 15, 1835, McLellin also served as a teacher of penmanship at the Kirtland School for Temporal Education in 1834 and as an assistant teacher at the School of the Prophets. He held membership on the high council in Clay County, Missouri, and briefly served as a captain in the Missouri State Militia in 1837. However, his apostolic tenure was brief; he was excommunicated on May 11, 1838, during a period of severe church-state conflict in Missouri.

mission.location: Eastern United States, Missouri, and Illinois

william-smith-1811.life_summary: William Smith was born March 13, 1811, in Royalton, Vermont, the eighth child of Joseph Smith Sr. and Lucy Mack Smith. He grew up in a financially struggling household and received minimal formal education. The family's economic hardship shaped much of his early life, though he was baptized into the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints on June 9, 1830, by David Whitmer. Smith worked in various capacities throughout his life, including civic service in Illinois. He eventually settled in Iowa, where he spent his final years. Smith's life was marked by significant ecclesiastical advancement in his youth followed by a dramatic and controversial fall from authority.
william-smith-1811.church_summary: William Smith was ordained an apostle on February 15, 1835, after his brother Joseph insisted on his selection despite objections from other church leaders. Following Hyrum Smith's death in 1844, William succeeded him as Presiding Patriarch in 1845. However, he encountered significant conflict with Brigham Young over the scope of his patriarchal authority. After expressing strong disagreement with church leadership, comparing Young to Pontius Pilate and Nero and accusing leaders of plural marriage practices, Smith was excommunicated on October 19, 1845. Rather than following Young to Utah, he initially affiliated with James J. Strang's Strangite movement and later joined the Reorganized Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints in 1878, remaining a high priest until his death.
